readingItems.topic: Alliance burden-sharing trade-off
readingItems.passage: NATO members must share costs. Countries with bigger economies pay more money. Smaller countries send more soldiers. This trade-off helps the alliance stay strong.
readingItems.question: What do smaller NATO countries do to help the alliance?

options.label: A
options.text: They send more soldiers to help.
options.rationale: KEY — correct. This paraphrases 'Smaller countries send more soldiers' by substituting the pronoun 'They' for the noun phrase 'Smaller countries' and adding 'to help', so it is not a verbatim lift while remaining accessible at A2 level.

options.label: B
options.text: They pay more money to the alliance.
options.rationale: Distractor — reversal error. The text states that countries with bigger economies pay more money. A weak reader may miss that this detail applies to larger, not smaller, members.

options.label: C
options.text: They buy new weapons for other members.
options.rationale: Distractor — outside-knowledge lure. Purchasing equipment is a plausible contribution to an alliance, but the text makes no mention of weapons or procurement; a candidate relying on general assumptions rather than the passage will be drawn here.

options.label: D
options.text: They ask larger countries for money.
options.rationale: Distractor — plausible misread. A candidate who notices that smaller countries and money appear in the same text might infer a dependency relationship that the passage does not describe, selecting this option in error.

readingItems.topic: Geopolitics & international relations — contested claim about sanctions effectiveness
readingItems.passage: Some countries put sanctions on other countries to stop bad actions. The US says its new sanctions on Country A work. But Country A says the sanctions do not work. Poor people suffer most.
readingItems.question: What does Country A say about the sanctions?

options.label: A
options.text: The sanctions help poor people in Country A.
options.rationale: Reversal distractor. The passage states 'poor people suffer most' — the opposite of being helped. A weak reader who notices 'poor people' but misses the negative framing may select this option.

options.label: B
options.text: The sanctions do not work.
options.rationale: CORRECT. The passage explicitly states 'Country A says the sanctions do not work.' Option B is a near-verbatim retrieval with the attribution tag removed, which is appropriate for Level 1 literal comprehension without being a word-for-word sentence copy.

options.label: C
options.text: The sanctions work, as the US says.
options.rationale: Attribution-swap distractor. This is the US position, not Country A's. A candidate who identifies the correct claim but assigns it to the wrong party — failing to track the two speakers — will choose this.

options.label: D
options.text: The sanctions stop bad actions.
options.rationale: Misattribution distractor. 'Stop bad actions' appears in the opening sentence as the stated purpose of sanctions in general, not as Country A's claim. A reader who pattern-matches 'sanctions' with this phrase without tracking who said what will choose this.

readingItems.topic: Energy transition and security of supply
readingItems.passage:
NOTICE TO RESIDENTS

The local gas power plant closes on 15 April. The new solar panels are not yet working. Until June, electricity may be limited between 6 pm and 10 pm.
readingItems.question: What happens to electricity between April and June?

options.label: A
options.text: It is cut off completely every night.
options.rationale: Distractor targeting an over-generalisation: a weak reader inflates 'may be limited' into 'cut off completely' and stretches the stated window (6 pm–10 pm) to 'every night'. Both elements exist in the text but are exaggerated beyond what is written.

options.label: B
options.text: It comes from the new solar panels.
options.rationale: Distractor targeting a plausible inference a weak reader might make: the notice mentions solar panels, so they assume the panels are supplying power. The passage says the opposite — the solar panels are 'not yet working', which is precisely why the gap exists.

options.label: C
options.text: It may be limited in the evenings.
options.rationale: Correct key. The passage states 'electricity may be limited between 6 pm and 10 pm.' 'In the evenings' is a natural, near-verbatim paraphrase of the stated hours, and 'may be limited' is carried over directly, satisfying the Level 1 literal-retrieval requirement without reproducing the sentence word for word.

options.label: D
options.text: It is more available after 6 pm.
options.rationale: Distractor targeting a reversal of effect: '6 pm' is lifted verbatim from the passage, but the relationship is inverted — the text says supply is limited after 6 pm, not that it becomes more available. A candidate who misreads 'limited' or confuses the sentence direction may choose this.

readingItems.topic: A shift in deterrence thinking
readingItems.passage: Military experts say deterrence is changing. In the past, countries used military force to prevent war. Now, economic tools are more important. Sanctions and trade restrictions can also stop conflicts.
readingItems.question: According to the text, what are countries relying on more now to prevent war?

options.label: A
options.text: Military force
options.rationale: Reversal distractor. The passage explicitly places military force in the past ('In the past, countries used military force'), not the present. A candidate who scans without tracking the temporal contrast may pick this.

options.label: B
options.text: Alliances with other nations
options.rationale: Plausible-assumption distractor. Alliances are a common real-world deterrence concept, so a candidate might assume they are the alternative to military force. The text never mentions them.

options.label: C
options.text: International courts
options.rationale: Plausible-assumption distractor. Candidates aware of bodies such as the UN or ICJ may associate conflict prevention with legal institutions. The passage does not mention courts or any legal mechanism.

options.label: D
options.text: Economic tools
options.rationale: KEY. The passage states directly: 'Now, economic tools are more important.' The question slightly paraphrases ('relying on more now') rather than lifting verbatim, but the answer is explicitly supported by the text.

readingItems.topic: Conscription versus professional forces
readingItems.passage: Some countries use conscription. This means all young people must join the army for one or two years. Other countries have professional forces. These soldiers choose to serve and receive a salary.
readingItems.question: According to the text, what is conscription?

options.label: A
options.text: A system where young people must join the army
options.rationale: Correct. The passage states that conscription means 'all young people must join the army.' Option A paraphrases this definition directly and is the only reading fully supported by the text.

options.label: B
options.text: A system where soldiers choose to serve and receive pay
options.rationale: Distractor targeting conflation of the two concepts. 'Choose to serve' and 'salary' both appear in the text, but in the sentence about professional forces, not conscription. A reader who does not track which description belongs to which system will select this.

options.label: C
options.text: A system where young people join the army for a salary
options.rationale: Distractor targeting a cross-sentence misread. 'Salary' comes from the professional-forces sentence; 'young people' comes from the conscription sentence. A fast or inattentive reader may blend the two and attach the salary detail to conscription.

options.label: D
options.text: A system where young people choose how long they serve
options.rationale: Distractor targeting a misread of 'must.' The phrase 'one or two years' does appear in the conscription sentence, but the text says young people must join — there is no element of choice. A reader who skips or misses the word 'must' may infer that duration is voluntary.

readingItems.topic: Economics — disputed inflation figures
readingItems.passage: The government says inflation is 3%. The central bank says it is 5%. They use different numbers to measure prices. People do not know which figure is correct.
readingItems.question: What does the central bank say the inflation rate is?

options.label: A
options.rationale: Distractor — this is the government's figure, not the central bank's. A weak reader who cannot keep the two institutions separate will confuse the two numbers stated in successive sentences and select the first one mentioned.

options.label: B
options.rationale: KEY — the passage states explicitly 'The central bank says it is 5%.' This is literal retrieval appropriate for Level 1; the answer is present in the text, though the reader must track which institution made which claim across two short sentences.

options.label: C
options.rationale: Distractor — not stated in the passage. A candidate who mentally averages the two figures mentioned (3% and 5%) arrives at 4%, a plausible arithmetic error rather than a direct misread.

options.label: D
options.rationale: Distractor — not stated in the passage. A candidate who misremembers the central bank's figure or rounds upward from outside general knowledge about inflation may plausibly select a value just above the ones in the text.

readingItems.topic: AI governance / dual-use technology — workplace access notice
readingItems.passage:
NOTICE
This AI program can help people, but it can also be dangerous. Only approved staff may use it. If you have a question, call the safety office.
readingItems.question: Who can use the AI program?

options.label: A
options.text: Everyone who works in the office
options.rationale: Distractor — a careless reader skips the word 'approved' and assumes the program is open to all office workers. The notice explicitly restricts access, so this is wrong.

options.label: B
options.text: Only the safety office staff
options.rationale: Distractor — the safety office is mentioned as a contact for questions, not as the authorised users of the program. A reader who conflates the two functions of the notice will choose this.

options.label: C
options.text: Only approved staff members
options.rationale: Key — the notice states 'Only approved staff may use it.' Option B restates this with minimal paraphrase ('members' added), which is the expected near-verbatim retrieval at Level 1.

options.label: D
options.text: Only managers and supervisors
options.rationale: Distractor — a plausible outside assumption that access to a restricted tool belongs to managers; the text never mentions managers or supervisors, so this cannot be derived from the passage.

readingItems.topic: Reassessment of a UN peacekeeping mission
readingItems.passage: The UN peacekeeping mission in Kanda has 500 soldiers. The mission began in 2020. This year, UN officials say the force is not large enough. They plan to add 300 more troops.
readingItems.question: What do UN officials plan to do with the mission in Kanda?

options.label: A
options.text: End the peacekeeping mission in Kanda
options.rationale: Incorrect. The text states that officials plan to add more troops, not to close the mission. A candidate who associates 'reassessment' or 'not large enough' with a decision to terminate may choose this distractor.

options.label: B
options.text: Transfer soldiers to a different country
options.rationale: Incorrect. The text contains no information about relocating the existing soldiers. A candidate who confuses 'add 300 more' with a movement of personnel from one place to another may be drawn to this option.

options.label: C
options.text: Reduce the mission to 300 soldiers
options.rationale: Incorrect. The number 300 appears in the text as the quantity of troops to be added, not as a new reduced total. A candidate who reads '300' in isolation without processing 'add' may misinterpret this as a cut.

options.label: D
options.text: Increase the size of the force
options.rationale: Correct. 'They plan to add 300 more troops' means the total force will grow, i.e., its size will increase. The option paraphrases the text rather than copying it word for word, requiring the candidate to match the idea rather than a specific phrase.

readingItems.topic: Migration policy and demographic need
readingItems.passage: This country has many old people but few young workers. It needs more workers. A new law, however, does not allow many people to come from other countries.
readingItems.question: What problem does this country have?

options.label: A
options.text: It does not have enough young workers.
options.rationale: KEY. The passage states directly that the country has 'few young workers' and 'needs more workers.' Option A paraphrases 'few young workers' as 'not enough young workers' — a minimal restatement, not a verbatim lift, making it the one defensible answer.

options.label: B
options.text: It does not have enough old people.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR. Reversal misread. The passage states the country has 'many old people,' not few. A weak reader who skims only the word 'old people' without processing 'many' may invert the quantity, producing this error.

options.label: C
options.text: Many young workers are leaving the country.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR. Direction-of-movement reversal. The passage discusses people being unable to enter the country, not residents departing. A weak reader may confuse the migration constraint with an emigration scenario, especially if they already associate 'few young workers' with people going away.

options.label: D
options.text: There are too many people from other countries.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR. Reversal of the migration detail. The new law restricts entry, implying arrivals are scarce — the opposite of 'too many.' A weak reader may assume a restrictive immigration law must respond to overcrowding, importing an outside assumption the text does not support.

readingItems.topic: Disinformation and Press Freedom
readingItems.passage: Some news stories are not true. This is a big problem. Some governments want to stop newspapers. But a free press helps people know the truth. Read more than one newspaper.
readingItems.question: According to the text, why is a free press important?

options.label: A
options.text: It stops people from reading newspapers.
options.rationale: Distractor — reversal. The text says some governments want to stop newspapers, not that a free press does so. A weak reader who scans 'stop newspapers' without tracking the subject may select this.

options.label: B
options.text: It helps people know the truth.
options.rationale: Key — correct. The text states directly 'a free press helps people know the truth.' The option paraphrases by removing the subject phrase (which the question already names), leaving only the stated benefit.

options.label: C
options.text: It tells governments what to do.
options.rationale: Distractor — plausible outside assumption. Both 'free press' and 'governments' appear in the text, so a weak reader may link them in this way, but the text never states this relationship.

options.label: D
options.text: It creates news stories that are not true.
options.rationale: Distractor — misattribution of the problem. The text says fake news (not a free press) produces untrue stories. A weak reader who does not track which noun phrase each sentence is about may assign the problem to the wrong actor.

readingItems.topic: Defence procurement trade-offs
readingItems.passage: The army needs new trucks and new radios. This year, it has money for only one item. It has decided to buy the trucks. The radios will be ordered next year.
readingItems.question: What will the army buy this year?

options.label: A
options.text: New radios only
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — targets a confusion between what is deferred and what is purchased. 'Radios' appears prominently twice, and the final sentence places it last; a weak reader who loses track of the sequence may remember 'radios' as the outcome rather than the item postponed.

options.label: B
options.text: New trucks and new radios
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — targets a reader who notices that both items are listed as needs ('The army needs new trucks and new radios') but overlooks or misreads the budget constraint ('money for only one item'). The assumption that all stated needs will be met makes this a plausible lure.

options.label: C
options.text: New trucks only
options.rationale: KEY — the passage explicitly states 'It has decided to buy the trucks,' and the budget constraint ('money for only one item') confirms that nothing else will be purchased this year. 'New trucks only' paraphrases this conclusion without lifting the exact sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: Neither trucks nor radios
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — targets a reader who over-generalises the budget limitation. Reading 'it has money for only one item' as a signal of severe financial shortage, a weak reader might conclude the army cannot buy anything at all, ignoring the explicit purchase decision that follows.

readingItems.topic: Climate-driven resource competition: a bilateral water dispute
readingItems.passage: WATER NOTICE — Two countries cannot agree about the river. Country A says the river is smaller because of the hot, dry weather. Country B wants more water from the river.
readingItems.question: What does Country A say about the river?

options.label: A
options.text: Country B is already taking too much of its water.
options.rationale: Distractor — misattributes the cause of the problem. The text says Country B *wants* more water, but does not say it is currently taking too much. A weak reader may conflate wanting more with already taking too much.

options.label: B
options.text: The two countries should share it equally.
options.rationale: Distractor — plausible commonsense resolution, but the text says only that the countries cannot agree; no proposal for equal sharing appears anywhere. A test-wise but inattentive reader may assume this is implied.

options.label: C
options.text: Country A needs more water for its people.
options.rationale: Distractor — swaps the subject; it is Country B that wants more water, not Country A. A careless reader may confuse which country wants more water, especially since both country names appear close together.

options.label: D
options.text: The hot, dry weather has made it smaller.
options.rationale: Key — this is a close paraphrase of 'the river is smaller because of the hot, dry weather', which is stated explicitly as Country A's position. The phrasing 'has made it smaller' lightly restructures the original without lifting it verbatim, which is appropriate for Level 1 literal retrieval.

readingItems.topic: Reshoring trade-off: resilience versus operating costs
readingItems.passage: Rising tariffs have pushed several large manufacturers to move production closer to home. This shift — known as reshoring — reduces dependence on distant suppliers but raises operating costs.
readingItems.question: According to the text, what is one consequence of reshoring for manufacturers?

options.label: A
options.text: Operating costs for manufacturers go up.
options.rationale: Key — directly paraphrases 'raises operating costs' in the second sentence. The conjunction 'but' marks this as an explicitly stated drawback of the reshoring shift.

options.label: B
options.text: Dependence on foreign suppliers increases.
options.rationale: Distractor — reverses the stated effect. The text says reshoring 'reduces dependence on distant suppliers', not that it increases dependence.

options.label: C
options.text: Tariffs on imported goods are eliminated.
options.rationale: Distractor — confuses cause and effect. The text says rising tariffs push manufacturers toward reshoring; reshoring does not remove tariffs.

options.label: D
options.text: Production quality improves at home factories.
options.rationale: Distractor — a plausible outside assumption about reshoring, but this effect is nowhere stated or implied in the passage.

readingItems.topic: Absence of a satellite-weapons treaty
readingItems.passage: More than 70 countries now operate satellites, yet no binding treaty limits their military use. As a result, several states continue to develop weapons designed to destroy satellites in orbit.
readingItems.question: According to the text, why do several states continue to develop weapons that can destroy satellites?

options.label: A
options.text: Most countries lack the technology to build such weapons.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — outside assumption; the text says nothing about other countries' technological capability. A candidate who misreads the passage as discussing a capability gap may choose this.

options.label: B
options.text: No international treaty limits the military use of satellites.
options.rationale: KEY — the passage states 'no binding treaty limits their military use' and links this directly to weapon development via 'as a result', making this a near-verbatim paraphrase of the explicitly stated cause.

options.label: C
options.text: Satellites in orbit are too expensive to protect.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — true-but-irrelevant; the text does not mention the cost of satellite protection. A candidate who supplies an outside economic rationale for anti-satellite development may choose this.

options.label: D
options.text: International agreements encourage states to strengthen their space defences.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — reversed logic; the passage argues the absence of treaties explains weapon development. A candidate who misreads 'no binding treaty' as positive treaty activity will choose this.

readingItems.topic: Boom-and-bust health funding cycles
readingItems.passage: Health spending typically rises during a pandemic, then falls sharply when the crisis passes. As a result, stockpiles and early-warning systems are often left underfunded.
readingItems.question: According to the passage, what happens to health spending after a pandemic ends?

options.label: A
options.text: It continues to rise for several years after the outbreak.
options.rationale: Reverses the passage's claim — the text states spending falls, not rises, once the crisis is over.

options.label: B
options.text: It is redirected toward building and expanding stockpiles.
options.rationale: Misreads the causal direction — stockpiles are described as a casualty of the spending fall, not a destination for redirected funds.

options.label: C
options.text: It drops sharply once the crisis has passed.
options.rationale: Correct — closely paraphrases 'falls sharply when the crisis passes'; the only option the passage directly supports.

options.label: D
options.text: It remains stable until the next outbreak begins.
options.rationale: An outside assumption the passage does not support; the text says spending falls, not that it holds steady.

readingItems.topic: Alliance burden-sharing trade-off
readingItems.passage: Many countries join military alliances and agree to share the cost of collective defence. However, not all members spend the same amount. Some wealthier nations pay more, covering the gaps left by smaller or less prosperous partners. This arrangement allows poorer members to benefit from security without committing as many resources to their own armed forces. The trade-off is clear: smaller members save money but depend heavily on their allies, while larger contributors carry a heavier financial burden. In recent years, this imbalance has caused tension, as major contributors have pressed others to increase their defence spending.
readingItems.question: What is the main trade-off described in the text?

options.label: A
options.text: Smaller members benefit from collective security but become more dependent on their wealthier allies.
options.rationale: KEY. The passage states that smaller members 'benefit from security without committing as many resources' yet 'depend heavily on their allies.' This option paraphrases both sides of the stated trade-off without reproducing the exact wording, requiring the reader to connect two sentences.

options.label: B
options.text: Wealthier nations reduce their own defence budgets once smaller members join the alliance.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR. Reverses the financial direction described. The text says wealthier nations pay more and 'cover gaps,' not that they spend less. A weak reader who skims for 'wealthier nations' and 'spending' may invert the relationship.

options.label: C
options.text: Larger contributors gain more influence in alliance decisions because they spend more money.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR. Plausible from general knowledge of how alliances function, but the text never mentions influence or decision-making power. This tests whether the candidate limits conclusions to what the passage actually states.

options.label: D
options.text: Smaller members are eventually required to match the spending levels of their wealthier partners.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR. Over-reads the final sentence. The text says larger contributors have 'pressed others to increase their defence spending,' but does not say smaller members must reach parity. A candidate who misinterprets 'pressed to increase' as 'required to match' will choose this option.

readingItems.topic: Contested claims about the effectiveness of economic sanctions
readingItems.passage: Economic sanctions are one of the most common tools that governments use to change the behaviour of other countries. Supporters argue that sanctions can force governments to negotiate by damaging their economies. Critics, however, say that the evidence does not support this claim. Several studies show that sanctions rarely achieve their stated goals and that ordinary citizens — not their leaders — tend to suffer the most. Governments often find ways to work around restrictions, and in some cases sanctions may even strengthen a regime by creating a sense of national unity against an outside threat.
readingItems.question: According to the passage, what do critics of sanctions argue?

options.label: A
options.text: Sanctions are effective because they force governments to negotiate by damaging their economies.
options.rationale: Incorrect. This is the supporters' position, not the critics'. A candidate who does not carefully distinguish between the two sides may select this option, especially since it appears early in the passage.

options.label: B
options.text: Sanctions tend to harm ordinary citizens more than their leaders and can even help a regime stay in power.
options.rationale: Correct. This synthesises the two main points of the critics' argument presented in the passage: that ordinary citizens bear the greatest cost, and that sanctions may strengthen rather than weaken a regime. Neither phrase is a verbatim lift from the text.

options.label: C
options.text: Studies confirm that sanctions consistently achieve their stated political goals in most cases.
options.rationale: Incorrect. This directly reverses the passage's meaning. The passage states that sanctions 'rarely achieve their stated goals'; a careless reader who loses track of the direction of the claim, or who confuses the existence of studies with what they show, may choose this option.

options.label: D
options.text: Sanctions work best when they target specific government officials rather than whole economies.
options.rationale: Incorrect. This is a plausible-sounding policy position that a candidate may draw from general knowledge or prior reading, but the passage makes no mention of targeted versus economy-wide sanctions. It does not answer the question from the text.

readingItems.topic: Energy transition and security of supply
readingItems.passage: Many governments are accelerating the shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy, but this transition creates a new challenge: ensuring a reliable power supply. Wind and solar farms generate electricity only when weather conditions allow, which means output can drop sharply during calm or cloudy periods. Until battery storage technology improves significantly, countries risk facing power shortages if they retire coal and gas plants too quickly. Some energy experts argue that moving too fast risks trading one vulnerability — dependence on imported oil and gas — for another: an unstable domestic grid.
readingItems.question: What is the main problem described in this text?

options.label: A
options.text: Countries should keep using coal and gas plants until battery technology has fully improved.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The text identifies a risk without prescribing what countries should do. A reader who confuses a description of risk with a policy recommendation may choose this option.

options.label: B
options.text: Battery storage has already made renewable energy a fully stable source of electricity.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The text states that battery storage needs to improve significantly, making clear the problem is not yet solved. This option reverses the passage's meaning, targeting a reader who skims too quickly.

options.label: C
options.text: Governments are becoming too reliant on imported wind turbines and solar panels.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The text warns about dependence on imported oil and gas as the existing vulnerability, not about imported renewable equipment. A reader who notices the word 'imported' but not the type of energy source may be drawn to this option.

options.label: D
options.text: Switching away from fossil fuels too quickly may leave countries without a reliable power supply.
options.rationale: Correct. The passage argues that retiring fossil fuels too fast risks power shortages and an unstable grid. This option paraphrases that central concern without lifting any sentence verbatim.

readingItems.topic: Security & defence policy: shift in deterrence thinking
readingItems.passage:
For decades, Western defence planners believed that large conventional forces — tanks, aircraft, and troops — were the primary tools of deterrence. The logic was simple: a country with a powerful military would discourage potential aggressors from attacking.

That thinking has been changing. Analysts now argue that cyber capabilities and economic sanctions can act as deterrents just as effectively as traditional military strength. A country able to disrupt an adversary's financial system or critical infrastructure may not need a larger army to maintain peace.

This shift has prompted several NATO members to review how they allocate their defence budgets, moving some spending from heavy equipment toward digital and economic tools.
readingItems.question: What is the main point the writer is making in this passage?

options.label: A
options.text: Western countries have abandoned their belief in conventional military deterrence.
options.rationale: Distractor — over-generalisation. The passage states the thinking 'has been changing,' not that conventional deterrence has been abandoned. A weak reader who focuses on the contrast between old and new ideas may interpret the shift too sweepingly.

options.label: B
options.text: Defence budgets are growing as NATO members invest in both old and new deterrence tools.
options.rationale: Distractor — distortion of a detail. The final sentence says members are reviewing how they allocate existing budgets and moving some spending, not that total budgets are increasing. A reader who skims the last paragraph may conflate reallocation with growth.

options.label: C
options.text: The understanding of what makes an effective deterrent has been shifting.
options.rationale: Key — paraphrase of the passage's central claim ('That thinking has been changing'). The option synthesises the argument across all three paragraphs without lifting any single sentence verbatim.

options.label: D
options.text: Cyber attacks are now considered the main threat that NATO countries need to deter.
options.rationale: Distractor — role reversal. The passage presents cyber capabilities as a tool that a country uses to deter others, not as the primary threat countries face. A reader who confuses 'deterrent tool' with 'threat to be deterred' will select this.

readingItems.topic: Conscription vs. professional forces in European defence policy
readingItems.passage: Several European governments are reconsidering compulsory military service after decades of relying on professional armies. The change is driven partly by concerns that volunteer forces, though highly trained, are simply too small to manage large-scale conflicts. Supporters of conscription argue that it builds a broader reserve of trained personnel and strengthens ties between the military and wider society. Critics, however, warn that conscripts are more expensive to train and less effective in modern warfare than career soldiers. The debate reflects growing uncertainty about the security environment along Europe's eastern borders.
readingItems.question: According to the passage, what do supporters of conscription argue in its favour?

options.label: A
options.text: It creates a larger pool of trained reserves and builds stronger connections between the military and society.
options.rationale: Correct. This paraphrases the supporters' argument stated in the third sentence: conscription 'builds a broader reserve of trained personnel and strengthens ties between the military and wider society.' The key requires the reader to match meaning across a paraphrase, not lift a verbatim phrase.

options.label: B
options.text: It trains soldiers more effectively for modern warfare than professional military service does.
options.rationale: Incorrect. This reverses a claim made by the critics, who warn that conscripts are less effective in modern warfare than career soldiers. A weak reader may confuse which side of the debate is associated with effectiveness and misattribute the point to supporters.

options.label: C
options.text: It costs governments less to implement than maintaining an all-volunteer professional army.
options.rationale: Incorrect. This reverses the critics' warning: the passage states that conscripts are more expensive to train, not cheaper. A weak reader who remembers 'cost' as a key word in the passage may misremember the direction of the claim.

options.label: D
options.text: It ensures that the burden of military service is distributed equally across society.
options.rationale: Incorrect. While the passage mentions that conscription 'strengthens ties between the military and wider society,' it does not say that service is shared fairly or equally. This is a plausible but unsupported inference; a weak reader may read 'strengthens ties' as implying equal burden-sharing.

readingItems.topic: Economics — disputed reading of inflation data
readingItems.passage: The government announced that inflation fell to 3.1% last month, calling this evidence that its economic policy is working. However, consumer groups and some economists disagree. They note that food and energy prices — the items ordinary households spend most of their money on — are still rising by more than 8% a year. The critics argue that the official headline figure appears lower because it averages in goods and services that typical families rarely purchase. For many people, they say, the real cost of living feels considerably higher than the published number suggests.
readingItems.question: Why do some economists and consumer groups challenge the government's interpretation of the inflation figures?

options.label: A
options.text: They believe the government has made calculation errors in its published data.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The critics do not accuse the government of arithmetic mistakes; their objection is to the methodology — specifically that the index averages in goods rarely bought by ordinary households. A weak reader may conflate 'criticism of the data' with 'calculation error,' making this a plausible but wrong choice.

options.label: B
options.text: They argue that the official figure does not capture what most households actually pay.
options.rationale: Correct. The passage states that food and energy prices — the main everyday spending of ordinary families — are still rising by over 8%, and that the headline figure looks lower because it includes rarely-purchased items. This option paraphrases both points without quoting either directly, requiring the reader to combine two sentences.

options.label: C
options.text: They want food and energy prices to fall before any official figures are released.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The critics make no demand that prices reach a certain level as a precondition for publishing data. A reader who skims the passage may register that the critics are concerned about food and energy prices and misread this as a call for policy action rather than a methodological objection.

options.label: D
options.text: They think the recent drop in inflation is temporary and will soon reverse.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The passage makes no mention of future trends or predictions about where inflation is heading. This is a plausible economic argument that sounds relevant but is simply not present in the text; a candidate importing outside knowledge may be drawn to it.

readingItems.topic: AI Governance and Dual-Use Technology
readingItems.passage:
Artificial intelligence (AI) tools created for everyday use can often be adapted for military or surveillance purposes. This is called "dual-use" technology. For example, facial recognition software was originally designed to unlock smartphones, but some governments have used it to track people in public spaces without their permission.

Experts say that clearer international rules are needed to prevent the misuse of such technology. At present, however, governments have made little progress in agreeing on shared standards. Without these rules, AI systems could threaten civil liberties and increase the risk of conflict between states.
readingItems.question: What is the writer's main concern about dual-use AI technology?

options.label: A
options.text: Facial recognition software has made smartphones significantly easier for everyday users to unlock.
options.rationale: Distractor — misreads the facial recognition example. The passage introduces it only to illustrate dual-use risk; it makes no claim about improved smartphone usability. A weak reader may focus on the concrete phone detail and miss its illustrative function.

options.label: B
options.text: Governments are currently spending too much money on the development of military AI systems.
options.rationale: Distractor — introduces the idea of excessive defence spending, which the passage never mentions. A candidate who assumes 'military use of AI' implies a budget argument may select this plausible but unsupported option.

options.label: C
options.text: International organisations have already reached agreement on how to regulate AI technology.
options.rationale: Distractor — directly reverses the passage's claim. The text states that governments have made 'little progress in agreeing on shared standards.' A careless or fast reader who scans for keywords ('international,' 'agree,' 'standards') without reading carefully may miss the negation.

options.label: D
options.text: AI tools designed for civilian use may be misused because clear international rules do not yet exist.
options.rationale: CORRECT — paraphrases the passage's central argument across both paragraphs: civilian-purpose AI can be repurposed (paragraph 1) and the absence of agreed international standards leaves it uncontrolled (paragraph 2). The key synthesises two sentences rather than lifting one verbatim.

readingItems.topic: Reassessment of a UN Peacekeeping Mission
readingItems.passage: The United Nations mission in Valoria has been in place for seven years, but a recent review suggests it may no longer be achieving its original goals. When the mission began, its primary task was to monitor a ceasefire between two armed groups. That ceasefire has held, but violence between local communities has increased in areas where peacekeepers are not deployed. The review recommends either expanding the mission's area of operations or handing responsibility to regional authorities. Officials warn that without such changes, the mission risks becoming a permanent fixture rather than a temporary solution to a specific conflict.
readingItems.question: According to the article, why is the peacekeeping mission no longer considered fully effective?

options.label: A
options.text: The ceasefire it was sent to monitor has broken down in several areas.
options.rationale: Distractor — misread of a specific sentence. The text states that the original ceasefire 'has held'. A weak reader may associate 'violence has increased' with a ceasefire failure and select this option.

options.label: B
options.text: Regional authorities have refused to cooperate with UN personnel.
options.rationale: Distractor — plausible outside assumption not supported by the text. The text mentions transferring responsibility to regional authorities as a possible remedy, but says nothing about any refusal or lack of cooperation.

options.label: C
options.text: Violence has increased in parts of the region where peacekeepers are not present.
options.rationale: Key — paraphrases 'violence between local communities has increased in areas where peacekeepers are not deployed'. This is the specific evidence the review cites, and requires reading two sentences in sequence rather than scanning a single phrase.

options.label: D
options.text: The mission has not been in place long enough to achieve measurable results.
options.rationale: Distractor — reversal of the text's meaning. The text says the mission has run for seven years and risks becoming a 'permanent fixture', indicating the concern is that it has lasted too long without adapting, not that it has had too little time.

readingItems.topic: Demographic ageing and immigration policy in Europe
readingItems.passage:
Many European countries face a serious demographic challenge: their populations are ageing rapidly, and fewer young workers are entering the labour market. Economists warn that without significant growth in the working-age population, pension systems and public services will come under severe financial pressure.

Yet several of these governments have recently tightened their immigration rules, making it harder for workers from outside the EU to settle and find employment. Critics argue that stricter entry controls directly conflict with the economic need for new labour. Supporters of the restrictions, however, maintain that rapid population change places too great a strain on public resources and social cohesion.
readingItems.question: According to the passage, what is the main concern of critics who oppose tighter immigration rules?

options.label: A
options.text: Tighter entry controls work against the economic need for more workers in ageing societies.
options.rationale: Correct key — paraphrases and synthesises both paragraphs. The opening establishes the demographic need for more working-age people, and the second paragraph states that critics see stricter entry rules as directly conflicting with that economic need. The answer is not lifted verbatim; it combines information across the two paragraphs.

options.label: B
options.text: Immigration restrictions cause the working-age population to grow too quickly.
options.rationale: Distractor — reverses the direction of the effect described in the text. The passage states that tighter rules make it harder for workers to enter, which would slow workforce growth, not accelerate it. A candidate who reads hastily may pick this up by associating 'immigration' and 'population growth' without checking the direction.

options.label: C
options.text: Ageing populations cannot sustain their pension systems unless birth rates also increase.
options.rationale: Distractor — introduces an idea not found in the text. The passage mentions pressure on pension systems but never discusses birth rates as a solution. A candidate who has background knowledge about demographic policy may find this plausible, but it cannot be derived from the passage alone.

options.label: D
options.text: Supporters of stricter rules have failed to consider the impact on public resources.
options.rationale: Distractor — reverses a detail from the text. The passage explicitly states that it is supporters of restrictions who cite the strain on public resources as their reason for favouring tighter rules. A candidate who confuses which side makes which argument will be attracted to this option.

readingItems.topic: Disinformation and press freedom
readingItems.passage: Some governments have introduced laws requiring social media companies to remove false information quickly. Supporters say these measures are necessary to protect the public from harmful lies. However, press freedom groups warn that the same laws could be used to silence journalists and independent voices. When authorities decide what is "false", they also gain the power to control what is "true". Critics argue that better media education, not government censorship, is the most effective way to fight disinformation without threatening free expression.
readingItems.question: What is the main concern raised by press freedom groups about anti-disinformation laws?

options.label: A
options.text: The laws will force social media companies to pay heavy fines.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Fines are never mentioned in the passage. A test-taker may select this by drawing on general knowledge of how laws are enforced, rather than on what the text actually says — a plausible outside assumption the passage does not support.

options.label: B
options.text: Governments may use these laws to control what the public is allowed to know.
options.rationale: Correct. The passage states that press freedom groups warn the laws could 'silence journalists and independent voices' and that authorities thereby gain 'the power to control what is true'. Option B synthesises both points without lifting any phrase verbatim, requiring the reader to connect two sentences in the text.

options.label: C
options.text: Social media companies are unable to remove false content quickly enough.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The passage states that laws require companies to remove false content quickly, but says nothing about whether companies are capable of meeting that requirement. A weak reader may confuse the existence of a removal requirement with an implied failure to comply.

options.label: D
options.text: Media education programmes have not been effective in reducing disinformation.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The passage mentions media education as a proposed alternative to censorship, but never claims that existing programmes have failed. A reader who skims only the final sentence may infer a failure that the text does not state, making this a true-but-irrelevant distractor that also misreads the passage's logic.

readingItems.topic: Defence Procurement Trade-offs
readingItems.passage: Many governments must choose between buying new military equipment and maintaining what they already have. When budgets are limited, spending money on advanced fighter jets or warships often means that older vehicles and systems receive less maintenance. As a result, some armed forces find themselves with modern weapons but ageing support infrastructure that cannot keep them fully operational. Defence analysts argue that a balanced approach — allocating funds to both new purchases and upkeep — produces more reliable forces than simply acquiring the latest technology. However, political pressure frequently favours visible new acquisitions over less newsworthy maintenance programmes.
readingItems.question: What is the main problem described in the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: Governments prioritise maintaining old equipment over purchasing new and more capable weapons systems.
options.rationale: Distractor — reverses the trade-off described in the passage. The text states that new purchases are favoured over maintenance, not the other way around. A candidate who misreads the direction of the problem, or who skims too quickly, may select this.

options.label: B
options.text: Modern fighter jets and warships are simply too costly for most armed forces to keep operational.
options.rationale: Distractor — the passage does not say that new equipment is too expensive to operate. The problem is that maintenance of older systems is underfunded, not that new platforms are unaffordable. A surface reader who focuses on 'fighter jets or warships' and 'operational' may conflate cost with affordability of new systems.

options.label: C
options.text: Political leaders tend to favour maintenance programmes over high-profile purchases of new weapons.
options.rationale: Distractor — directly reverses the political dynamic stated in the passage. The text says political pressure favours 'visible new acquisitions over less newsworthy maintenance programmes'. A careless reader may misread the direction of this contrast and select this option.

options.label: D
options.text: Investing in new military equipment often leaves less funding available to maintain existing systems.
options.rationale: Key — this paraphrases the central trade-off without reproducing any verbatim phrase. The passage explains that limited budgets force a choice, and that spending on new items means older vehicles and infrastructure receive less upkeep, leading to reliability problems.

readingItems.topic: Dispute over river water rights amid climate-driven scarcity
readingItems.passage: Two neighbouring countries in Central Asia have been arguing over rights to the Kara River for several years. As rising temperatures reduce the mountain snowpack that feeds the river, less water reaches farmers in the lower valley. The upstream country wants to build a new dam to store water for its own agricultural needs. The downstream country strongly opposes the plan, saying the dam would leave its farmers without enough water to grow food. International mediators have tried to bring the two governments to the table, but no agreement has been reached so far.
readingItems.question: According to the passage, why does the downstream country oppose the dam project?

options.label: A
options.text: It believes the dam will cause flooding in the lower valley.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The passage does not mention flooding at any point. A candidate may associate dams in general with flood risk and select this option, but there is no textual basis for it.

options.label: B
options.text: It wants to build its own dam on the river to store water.
options.rationale: Incorrect. It is the upstream country, not the downstream one, that wants to build a dam. A careless reader who does not track which country holds which position may reverse the roles and choose this option.

options.label: C
options.text: It believes the dam would reduce the water available to its farmers.
options.rationale: Correct. The passage states that the downstream country says the dam 'would leave its farmers without enough water to grow food.' This option paraphrases that stated concern — less water reaching farmers — without reproducing the wording verbatim.

options.label: D
options.text: It thinks international mediators are favouring the upstream country.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The passage says mediators have not yet produced an agreement, but says nothing about the downstream country distrusting or criticising the mediators. A candidate might infer bias from the failed talks, but the text does not support this.

readingItems.topic: Friend-shoring: resilience versus efficiency trade-off
readingItems.passage: For decades, global manufacturers chased efficiency by concentrating production in the lowest-cost locations, creating supply chains of remarkable output but alarming fragility. The disruptions of the early 2020s exposed this trade-off: single-source suppliers for critical components left industries unable to respond when borders closed or political relations soured. Governments have since pushed to diversify sourcing toward trusted partners — a strategy branded 'friend-shoring' — even though the resulting redundancy raises production costs. The gain in resilience, proponents argue, is worth that premium because a supply chain that breaks under stress is not, in fact, efficient.
readingItems.question: What is the main argument the passage makes about the friend-shoring strategy?

options.label: A
options.text: It is worthwhile because a supply chain that fails under pressure is not genuinely efficient.
options.rationale: Correct: paraphrases the passage's closing argument — that the resilience premium is justified because a fragile supply chain cannot be considered truly efficient. This synthesises the final sentence without lifting it verbatim.

options.label: B
options.text: It reduces costs by replacing single-source suppliers with a broader network of trusted partners.
options.rationale: Distractor: reverses the passage's explicit claim. The text states that friend-shoring's redundancy raises production costs, not lowers them. A candidate who reads quickly may conflate 'diversify sourcing' with 'reduce costs'.

options.label: C
options.text: It became necessary when governments closed borders during the early-2020s disruptions.
options.rationale: Distractor: true-but-irrelevant. Border closures are cited as context for the disruptions that exposed supply-chain fragility, not as the argument for why friend-shoring is worthwhile. A candidate who identifies the border-closure detail may mistake it for the main point.

options.label: D
options.text: It demonstrates that resilience and cost efficiency in global supply chains cannot coexist.
options.rationale: Distractor: over-generalises. The passage frames resilience and efficiency as a trade-off requiring a deliberate cost-benefit judgement, not as goals that are mutually exclusive in all circumstances.

readingItems.topic: Space governance — great-power reluctance to accept binding treaty limits
readingItems.passage: Low Earth orbit is growing dangerously crowded. The number of active satellites has tripled in less than a decade, and debris from defunct spacecraft and anti-satellite weapons tests now threatens functioning systems. Several states have called for a binding international treaty to restrict such tests and regulate orbital use. Progress, however, has been slow: countries that rely most heavily on satellites for military and commercial purposes are reluctant to accept any rules that might constrain their own programmes. The result is a domain managed only by voluntary guidelines that few states follow consistently.
readingItems.question: According to the passage, what is the main reason that efforts to agree on a space treaty have made little progress?

options.label: A
options.text: The rapid expansion of satellite networks has made it too complex for negotiators to identify which systems most need protection.
options.rationale: Distractor targeting a misread: the passage mentions the growth in satellite numbers as background context for congestion, but does not identify this complexity as the reason treaty negotiations have stalled. The stated reason is political reluctance, not a technical classification problem.

options.label: B
options.text: The nations with the greatest military and commercial stake in satellite systems oppose binding commitments that might restrict their activities.
options.rationale: Correct. The passage states that 'countries that rely most heavily on satellites for military and commercial purposes are reluctant to accept any rules that might constrain their own programmes.' This option paraphrases that cause without lifting the sentence verbatim.

options.label: C
options.text: Voluntary codes of conduct have so far proved effective enough to reduce orbital congestion without formal regulation.
options.rationale: Distractor exploiting a reversal: the passage says the opposite — voluntary guidelines exist but 'few states follow consistently,' implying they are inadequate. A hasty reader who notes that voluntary guidelines exist may miss that the text presents them as a failed substitute, not a success.

options.label: D
options.text: International bodies lack the authority to monitor or enforce any agreement covering activities in outer space.
options.rationale: Distractor based on a plausible outside assumption: while enforcement of space law is widely discussed, the passage does not mention lack of institutional authority as a reason for stalled progress. The stated obstacle is the unwillingness of key states, not any organisational limitation.

readingItems.topic: Boom-and-bust cycles in pandemic preparedness funding
readingItems.passage: Health systems in many countries follow a boom-and-bust pattern in pandemic preparedness spending. After a major outbreak, governments increase budgets, stockpile supplies, and expand surveillance networks. Once the immediate crisis fades, however, funding typically falls back to pre-crisis levels and stockpiles are allowed to run down. The result is a cycle in which systems are well-resourced when a threat has already passed but under-resourced when the next one arrives. Experts argue that shifting to sustained baseline funding would break this cycle and give early-warning systems the continuity they need to function reliably.
readingItems.question: What is the main point the writer makes about pandemic preparedness funding?

options.label: A
options.text: Governments achieve the best outcomes by increasing spending immediately after an outbreak ends.
options.rationale: Distractor — misreads the passage's description of post-crisis spending increases as an endorsement. The passage criticises this pattern: rising spending after a threat has passed still leaves systems under-resourced for the next one.

options.label: B
options.text: Stockpiling supplies before an outbreak is the most reliable way to prevent future health emergencies.
options.rationale: Distractor — the passage mentions stockpiling as part of post-crisis action, not pre-crisis prevention. 'Before an outbreak' reverses the timing stated in the text, and 'most reliable way to prevent' goes well beyond anything the passage claims.

options.label: C
options.text: Early-warning systems are currently too expensive for most governments to maintain year after year.
options.rationale: Distractor — the passage states that sustained funding would give early-warning systems 'the continuity they need to function reliably,' implying a lack of continuity, but it never attributes this to cost. The 'too expensive' claim is an outside assumption the text does not support.

options.label: D
options.text: Preparedness funding typically rises after a crisis but then drops again, leaving systems poorly equipped for the next outbreak.
options.rationale: Key — paraphrases the central argument in sentences 2–4: governments boost investment after a crisis, funding subsequently returns to pre-crisis levels, and the result is a cycle in which systems are under-resourced when the next threat arrives.

readingItems.topic: Security & Defence Policy — Alliance Burden-Sharing
readingItems.passage:
The debate over defence burden-sharing within NATO has long been framed in terms of arithmetic: which members spend two percent of their gross domestic product on defence, and which do not. Yet this framing, while politically convenient, obscures a more uncomfortable trade-off that smaller alliance members routinely face.

For states with limited budgets, reaching the two-percent threshold often means diverting resources from capabilities that directly serve national security — border management, intelligence, cyber resilience — in favour of hardware procurement that satisfies the metric but may be of limited operational utility. A Baltic state that purchases main battle tanks to demonstrate fiscal compliance signals commitment to allies while arguably diluting its own most relevant defence competencies, which lie in asymmetric and territorial resistance.

Conversely, a member that openly falls short of the numerical target risks a different cost: it invites the narrative of free-riding, eroding the political goodwill on which extended deterrence ultimately depends. The guarantee of collective defence is, at its core, a political compact, and members perceived as insufficiently committed find their requests for forward basing or rapid reinforcement treated with greater scepticism.

The uncomfortable implication is that the two-percent benchmark, whatever its strategic merits, functions as much as a loyalty signal as a measure of genuine military contribution. Smaller members are thus caught between two rational imperatives: optimise spending for their own operational context, or optimise for alliance optics. The difficulty is that, in the short term, these imperatives frequently point in opposite directions.
readingItems.question: Which of the following best captures the author's central argument about the two-percent benchmark?

options.label: A
options.text: By acting primarily as a political signal, the benchmark may push smaller members toward spending decisions that are poorly matched to their own operational requirements.
options.rationale: Correct. The passage argues that the benchmark 'functions as much as a loyalty signal as a measure of genuine military contribution' and illustrates how meeting it can lead smaller states to purchase hardware of limited operational value. This option synthesises both the signalling function identified in the final paragraph and the capability trade-off introduced in the second, without lifting any phrase verbatim.

options.label: B
options.text: Smaller members that exceed the spending target thereby demonstrate stronger strategic judgement than those that fall short.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The passage implies the opposite: members that spend heavily to reach the threshold may be prioritising hardware of 'limited operational utility,' meaning numerical compliance is not equated with strategic wisdom. A weak reader who assumes meeting the target is inherently positive will be drawn to this option.

options.label: C
options.text: The benchmark would be a reliable gauge of military readiness if it were combined with a systematic assessment of the quality of the hardware procured.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The passage does not propose this methodological refinement; it diagnoses a structural dilemma rather than recommending a particular fix. This distractor appeals to a candidate who misreads the author's critique as a call for a modified metric rather than a fundamental tension between two rational imperatives.

options.label: D
options.text: Free-riding has grown so prevalent among smaller members that the benchmark's credibility as a foundation of deterrence has been permanently undermined.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The passage acknowledges the political costs of the free-riding narrative but does not claim that free-riding is widespread or that deterrence credibility has been irreparably damaged. This distractor tempts a reader who over-extends the argument of the third paragraph, inflating a structural risk into a definitive collapse.

readingItems.topic: Geopolitics & International Relations — contested claims about sanctions effectiveness
readingItems.passage:
The conventional verdict on economic sanctions — that they rarely compel the behavioural change they are designed to produce — rests on a measurement problem that their critics have been slow to acknowledge. Most empirical assessments compare the imposition of sanctions against a single outcome: whether the targeted government capitulated on the specific demand that triggered the measures. By that narrow standard, the record is indeed poor. Sanctions against Iran did not immediately halt nuclear enrichment; those against Russia did not reverse territorial annexation. Yet this framing, however intuitively appealing, mistakes one possible function of sanctions for the only one.

Sanctions serve a portfolio of purposes beyond compellence. They signal alliance cohesion, imposing political costs on any member state tempted to defect from a coalition. They preserve the credibility of international norms by demonstrating that violations carry tangible consequences, even where those consequences fall short of capitulation. And they gradually erode the economic base from which an adversarial state projects power — a long-term constraint that is genuinely difficult to measure within a two- or three-year study window.

None of this is to claim that sanctions are reliably effective instruments. Poorly designed regimes leak through third-party intermediaries; prolonged measures can entrench the very elites they target while disproportionately burdening civilian populations. The honest conclusion is that effectiveness depends heavily on design, coalition unity, and the specificity of the demand being made. The debate, however, is poorly served by studies that reduce a multi-purpose instrument to a single metric and declare it a failure.
readingItems.question: What does the author identify as the fundamental flaw in most empirical assessments of sanctions effectiveness?

options.label: A
options.text: The studies use an excessively narrow timeframe, missing the gradual erosion of an adversary's economic base.
options.rationale: Distractor — true-but-partial misread. The passage does mention that long-term attrition is 'genuinely difficult to measure within a two- or three-year study window,' and a candidate who fixates on the final sentence of paragraph two may select this. However, the timeframe issue is presented as a subsidiary illustration of a broader measurement error, not its primary source. The author's core objection — stated explicitly in paragraph one — is the single-metric problem, not the study horizon.

options.label: B
options.text: The studies underestimate the difficulty of sustaining coalition unity, which is the foundation of any effective sanctions regime.
options.rationale: Distractor — confusion of a condition for effectiveness with a flaw in measurement. Coalition unity is mentioned in paragraphs two and three as a prerequisite for sanctions to work, but the author never claims that empirical studies underestimate this difficulty. A candidate who conflates 'what makes sanctions succeed' with 'what the studies get wrong' will be drawn to this option.

options.label: C
options.text: The studies apply a single success criterion — regime capitulation — to an instrument that serves multiple distinct purposes.
options.rationale: Key. This synthesises the argument developed across paragraphs one and two. The author explicitly states that conventional assessments measure sanctions against 'a single outcome' (capitulation) and thereby 'mistake one possible function of sanctions for the only one.' Paragraphs one and two together enumerate the overlooked purposes — signalling, norm enforcement, long-term attrition — making this the author's identified fundamental flaw. The option paraphrases the text rather than lifting it verbatim.

options.label: D
options.text: The studies conflate the burden imposed on civilian populations with political pressure on the ruling elite.
options.rationale: Distractor — a misread that combines two separate details from paragraph three into a causal claim the author does not make. The passage does note that prolonged sanctions 'entrench the very elites they target while disproportionately burdening civilian populations,' but this is raised as a design flaw of the sanctions themselves, not as an analytical error in how studies evaluate them. A candidate who scans for the passage's most concrete paired contrast may be misled here.

readingItems.topic: Energy transition and security of supply
readingItems.passage:
The accelerating drive to decarbonise electricity grids has introduced a paradox that energy planners are only beginning to confront in full. Renewables, by their nature, generate power when conditions allow rather than when demand dictates. Solar panels are idle at night; wind turbines fall silent in still air. For decades, fossil-fuel baseload plants absorbed these fluctuations without incident. As those plants are progressively retired, the margin between available supply and peak demand narrows in ways that conventional capacity forecasts do not always capture.

Battery storage and cross-border grid interconnections are the prescribed remedies, yet both remain constrained. Utility-scale battery installations, while growing rapidly, cover only a fraction of the storage volumes that a fully renewable grid would require during prolonged low-generation periods. Interconnectors, meanwhile, depend on neighbouring countries exporting surplus power at precisely the moment when domestic shortfalls occur — an assumption that breaks down during continent-wide weather events affecting multiple grids simultaneously.

Governments have responded unevenly. Some have negotiated long-term contracts for liquefied natural gas as a transitional bridge, accepting renewed fossil-fuel dependency in exchange for guaranteed dispatchable capacity. Others have extended the operational licences of nuclear plants that had been scheduled for decommissioning, a reversal that provokes fierce domestic debate but which analysts broadly view as the most carbon-efficient stopgap available. What unites both responses is an implicit acknowledgement that the pace of transition has outrun the infrastructure needed to sustain it — and that energy security, once treated as a solved problem in stable democracies, has reasserted itself as a first-order political concern.
readingItems.question: What does the author imply is the fundamental reason why governments have resorted to LNG contracts and nuclear licence extensions?

options.label: A
options.text: The retirement of fossil-fuel baseload plants has made reliable generation permanently dependent on dispatchable thermal capacity.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — over-generalisation and distortion. The passage notes that retiring fossil-fuel plants narrows supply margins, but frames this as a transitional management problem, not evidence that thermal capacity is permanently indispensable. The word 'permanently' goes well beyond what the text supports and inverts the author's argument, which concerns a gap in infrastructure rather than an inherent ceiling on renewables.

options.label: B
options.text: Battery storage and interconnector projects have been consistently underfunded in national energy plans.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — invented cause. The passage acknowledges that batteries and interconnectors are constrained and insufficient at scale, but attributes this to technical and logistical limitations, not to deliberate or consistent underfunding. A candidate who reads the second paragraph loosely may infer governmental negligence, but the text provides no such basis.

options.label: C
options.text: Energy security had been treated as a largely unproblematic issue in stable democracies for much of the preceding period.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — true-but-irrelevant. The passage does state that energy security was 'once treated as a solved problem in stable democracies,' making this option textually grounded and attractive. However, it describes a prior historical attitude rather than the cause of current policy choices. A candidate who confuses background context with causal explanation will select this option.

options.label: D
options.text: Renewable deployment has moved ahead of the storage and grid infrastructure needed to ensure reliable supply.
options.rationale: KEY — correct inference. The final sentence of the passage states explicitly that both governmental responses share 'an implicit acknowledgement that the pace of transition has outrun the infrastructure needed to sustain it.' Option B paraphrases this synthesis without lifting the wording verbatim, and it is the only option derivable from that concluding claim.

readingItems.topic: Security & defence policy — the shift from Cold War mutual restraint to integrated deterrence
readingItems.passage:
For most of the Cold War, deterrence was a relatively tractable concept. Two superpowers, each capable of inflicting catastrophic nuclear punishment on the other, were bound by a grim logic of mutual restraint. Strategic stability rested on the credibility of the threat, and credibility, in turn, rested on the adversary's certainty that retaliation would follow any first strike. The mathematics of annihilation were, paradoxically, a source of order.

That architecture has not disappeared, but it has been complicated beyond recognition. Contemporary defence planners now speak of "integrated deterrence" — a framework that layers nuclear capabilities with conventional force, cyber operations, space assets, and what strategists call "informational instruments of power." The concept reflects genuine changes in the security environment: adversaries increasingly operate in grey zones, testing resolve through ambiguous provocations that fall below the threshold of armed conflict and thus below the threshold of any credible nuclear response.

Yet the conceptual expansion carries its own risks. A deterrence framework that encompasses everything — from missile silos to social-media influence campaigns — risks becoming so broad as to lose its analytical purchase. Deterrence works when the threatened party understands precisely what is being deterred, why the threat would succeed, and what the costs of failure would be. The more variables introduced, the harder it becomes to satisfy any of those conditions. Some strategists worry, quietly, that "integrated deterrence" is less a coherent doctrine than a convenient label for a set of capabilities that have yet to be woven into a genuine theory of coercive restraint.

Whether this ambiguity is transitional — the necessary untidiness of a discipline adapting to a changing threat landscape — or structural remains the central unresolved question in contemporary strategic studies.
readingItems.question: What does the author imply about the concept of "integrated deterrence"?

options.label: A
options.text: It represents a coherent evolution of classical deterrence theory that is well suited to contemporary threats.
options.rationale: Distractor targeting readers who focus on the passage's concession in paragraph two — that the concept 'reflects genuine changes in the security environment' — and do not register the author's sustained critique in paragraphs three and four. The passage ultimately implies the opposite: coherence is precisely what the framework may lack.

options.label: B
options.text: Its breadth may erode the very clarity on which effective deterrence depends.
options.rationale: KEY. The author argues in paragraph three that a framework encompassing 'everything' risks losing its 'analytical purchase' and making it impossible to satisfy the three stated conditions of effective deterrence (precision about what is deterred, why the threat is credible, and what failure costs). This option paraphrases that inference without reproducing the passage's wording.

options.label: C
options.text: It over-prioritises nuclear capabilities at the expense of cyber and conventional instruments.
options.rationale: Distractor that reverses the direction of the argument. The passage presents integrated deterrence as adding cyber, conventional, and space elements to the nuclear baseline — the critique is that the framework is too inclusive, not too narrowly nuclear. A reader who skims paragraph two without tracking the logical direction of the shift may select this option.

options.label: D
options.text: Its shortcomings are openly acknowledged by the defence community as a fundamental doctrinal failure.
options.rationale: Distractor that over-reads the strength and visibility of the criticism. The passage says 'some strategists worry, quietly' — the qualifier 'quietly' signals that the concern is understated and minority-held, not widely or openly declared. A reader who extrapolates from the critique in paragraph three without attending to that hedging may choose this option.

readingItems.topic: Conscription versus professional forces in European security
readingItems.passage:
The return of conscription to the European security debate is less a reversal of doctrine than an admission that decades of professional-force orthodoxy left several allies structurally exposed. After the Cold War, the logic of professionalisation was compelling: smaller, better-trained, better-equipped formations could substitute for mass; quality, it was argued, would reliably defeat quantity. For two decades that calculus held — in expeditionary campaigns where technological superiority and air power could offset numbers, the professional model delivered. What it could not deliver, and what the return of high-intensity territorial conflict has now exposed, was strategic depth.

A conscript army, its critics long maintained, degrades unit cohesion and absorbs disproportionate resources in training recruits who will serve briefly and rotate out. The counter-argument, increasingly heard in Nordic and Baltic capitals, is that universal service generates something the market cannot purchase: a population that can be rapidly mobilised, that understands basic military procedure, and that regards defence as a civic obligation rather than a career choice. Finland's retention of conscription throughout the post-Cold War period — an outlier choice then, a template now — illustrates that the professional model's efficiency gains were purchased at the cost of resilience.

The debate is therefore not simply about force structure; it concerns the relationship between the state and its citizens in an era when the boundary between war and peace has grown permeable. Whether governments elect to restore mandatory service or opt for expanded voluntary reserve schemes, the assumption that a small professional cadre can bear the entire burden of national defence now commands little credibility.
readingItems.question: Which of the following best captures the author's implied position on the conscription debate?

options.label: A
options.text: The professional model's operational advantages do not offset the strategic vulnerability created by its limited manpower reserves.
options.rationale: Key — synthesis and inference. The author concedes that professional forces 'delivered' in expeditionary contexts but insists that what they 'could not deliver was strategic depth,' and concludes that their 'efficiency gains were purchased at the cost of resilience.' Option B paraphrases this core argument, integrating claims across all three paragraphs without lifting any phrase verbatim.

options.label: B
options.text: Conscription is the only viable response to high-intensity territorial conflict in contemporary Europe.
options.rationale: Distractor — over-generalisation.
