The author is sympathetic to conscription's merits but explicitly acknowledges 'expanded voluntary reserve schemes' as a credible alternative in the final paragraph. A candidate who reads the author's critical stance toward the professional model as an unqualified endorsement of mandatory service may be misled into this option.

options.label: C
options.text: Professional and conscript armies are broadly equivalent in effectiveness, provided both are adequately resourced.
options.rationale: Distractor — contradicts the text. The author explicitly differentiates between the two models' performance profiles: professional forces excelled in expeditionary campaigns but lacked resilience for territorial conflict. A candidate who mistakes the passage's balanced, analytical register for an even-handed verdict — rather than a structured argument leading to a conclusion — may be drawn to this option.

options.label: D
options.text: The return of conscription reflects a political failure to sustain public support for professional defence establishments.
options.rationale: Distractor — reverses the author's framing. The author presents the re-emergence of conscription as a rational strategic response to an exposed doctrine, not as a symptom of political weakness or public disillusionment. A candidate who misreads 'whether governments elect to restore mandatory service' as signalling reluctance, rather than acknowledging a genuine policy choice, may incorrectly infer that the author views the trend negatively.

readingItems.topic: Disputed readings of inflation data and their implications for monetary policy
readingItems.passage:
When the government's statistical office announced last autumn that consumer price inflation had fallen to 2.3 per cent, finance ministers across three countries declared the tightening cycle over and began signalling imminent rate cuts. The relief was genuine but, critics argued, premature. The headline figure, calculated on a consumer price index weighted towards goods, had been dragged down partly by a sharp fall in energy prices — a component that, as energy analysts know well, is as liable to reverse as it is to decline. Strip out energy and food and what remains — core inflation — was running at nearly twice the headline rate.

The dispute is not merely technical. Those who accept the headline number at face value tend to favour loosening monetary policy quickly, arguing that to do otherwise risks tipping an already fragile economy into recession. Those who emphasise core inflation counter that cutting rates while underlying price pressures remain elevated would simply embed inflation expectations and force a more painful correction later. The two camps are not divided by incompetence but by a genuine disagreement about which abstraction best captures economic reality.

What makes the debate intractable is that neither camp can be easily falsified in the short run. Energy prices may stay low, vindicating the optimists; or they may rebound, proving the sceptics right. In the meantime, central banks are left navigating by instruments that, depending on which economist is consulted, are either pointing in opposite directions or measuring entirely different things.
readingItems.question: Which of the following best reflects the author's assessment of the dispute between those who favour headline inflation and those who favour core inflation?

options.label: A
options.text: Policymakers who moved to cut rates on the basis of the headline figure were reckless, since energy price volatility was already well understood at the time.
options.rationale: Distractor — misreads tone and degree. The text characterises the early rate-cut signalling as 'premature' (a critics' judgement), not 'reckless,' and does not assert that policymakers ignored known volatility; it only notes that energy analysts are aware of the tendency for prices to reverse. A reader who over-reads the critical undertone of the opening paragraph may amplify the implied censure into an explicit accusation of recklessness.

options.label: B
options.text: The debate will ultimately be resolved once energy prices stabilise and headline and core inflation figures begin to converge.
options.rationale: Distractor — imposes a false resolution not present in the text. The final paragraph explicitly offers two equally possible outcomes — prices stay low or they rebound — without predicting convergence or settlement. A reader seeking a tidy conclusion may project this resolution onto the deliberately open-ended final paragraph.

options.label: C
options.text: The disagreement stems from a genuine methodological problem and cannot easily be settled by examining near-term economic data alone.
options.rationale: Key — correct. This paraphrases and synthesises two separate points from the passage: that the dispute reflects 'a genuine disagreement about which abstraction best captures economic reality,' and that 'neither camp can be easily falsified in the short run.' Neither phrase is lifted verbatim; the reader must combine both to reach this conclusion.

options.label: D
options.text: Despite its significant policy consequences, the distinction between headline and core inflation is ultimately too abstract to drive concrete monetary decisions.
options.rationale: Distractor — directly inverts the passage's argument. The entire second paragraph is devoted to showing that the choice between the two measures has very real and opposing policy prescriptions (rate cuts versus rate holds), with concrete consequences including recession risk and embedded inflation expectations. A reader who attends only to the word 'abstraction' in the text and misses the surrounding argument about stakes may select this option.

readingItems.topic: AI governance and dual-use technology
readingItems.passage:
The rapid commercial deployment of large language models and autonomous decision-making systems has exposed a critical gap in existing technology governance frameworks. Unlike nuclear or chemical weapons, which require specialised industrial infrastructure detectable by international inspectors, artificial intelligence systems capable of sophisticated analysis or autonomous action can be developed in ordinary data centres, updated incrementally, and transferred across borders as compressed files. The dual-use character of AI — its simultaneous applicability to civilian and military ends — is not an exceptional feature but its defining one.

Multilateral export-control regimes, designed in an era of tangible military hardware, have struggled to adapt. Proposals to restrict the export of high-performance chips have generated some traction, yet critics argue that focusing on hardware alone is akin to regulating the sale of printing presses while ignoring the manuscripts. The underlying algorithms, training methodologies, and datasets that determine a model's capabilities remain largely unconstrained. A state or non-state actor denied access to leading-edge silicon may still fine-tune a capable open-source model on commodity hardware for intelligence analysis, disinformation campaigns, or autonomous weapons guidance.

Advocates of a precautionary approach contend that governance must shift upstream — towards obligations on developers and cloud providers to evaluate military applicability before deployment. Sceptics counter that no definition of "dual-use" in this domain has yet proved sufficiently precise to be enforceable without paralysing legitimate research. The impasse is revealing: the architecture of international arms control was built for a world in which military and civilian technologies were distinguishable. Artificial intelligence was not designed with that distinction in mind.
readingItems.question: What does the passage imply is the fundamental obstacle to effective AI governance?

options.label: A
options.text: Existing export-control regimes cannot be effectively updated because they were designed to track physical military hardware rather than software.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — misread targeting the second paragraph. The passage does state that export-control regimes 'were designed in an era of tangible military hardware' and 'have struggled to adapt,' so A is anchored in the text. However, it identifies only a mechanical shortcoming (outdated instruments) and stops short of the author's deeper diagnosis: the entire conceptual premise of arms control — that military and civilian technologies are distinguishable — does not hold for AI. A reader who focuses on the second paragraph without integrating the argument of the third will select this option.

options.label: B
options.text: International agreement on restricting high-performance chips has stalled because leading technology companies have resisted such measures.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — reversal and unsupported attribution. The passage states that chip-restriction proposals have 'generated some traction,' which directly contradicts C's claim that consensus has stalled. Furthermore, the passage attributes the insufficiency of chip controls to their inherent technical limitations (capable open-source models can be run on commodity hardware), not to industry resistance. A candidate who conflates 'critics argue it is insufficient' with 'companies have opposed it' will be drawn to this option.

options.label: C
options.text: The proliferation of open-source AI models has made traditional arms-control verification methods technically unworkable.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — over-generalisation from a specific example. The passage cites open-source model proliferation as one illustration of how chip restrictions can be circumvented, but it does not claim that verification methods have become technically unworkable as a general conclusion. This distractor tempts candidates who read a single illustrative example as the author's overarching thesis, ignoring the broader conceptual argument developed in the final paragraph.

options.label: D
options.text: The dual-use nature of AI is intrinsic to the technology itself, making it structurally incompatible with governance frameworks premised on clear military-civilian distinctions.
options.rationale: KEY — the passage's central argument assembles two complementary claims: first, that AI's dual-use character is definitional ('not an exceptional feature but its defining one'), and second, that the architecture of arms control 'was built for a world in which military and civilian technologies were distinguishable' — a condition AI does not satisfy. B synthesises these across paragraphs without reproducing the text verbatim, correctly identifying the conceptual mismatch as the fundamental obstacle rather than any single policy gap.

readingItems.topic: Security & defence policy — reassessment of a peacekeeping mandate
readingItems.passage:
A decade after its deployment, the United Nations mission in the region faces a reassessment that goes beyond logistics and budget lines. For years, the mission's advocates argued that its presence served as an indispensable buffer, preventing a resumption of open hostilities between parties whose grievances remained unresolved. Critics now contend that this very logic has become self-defeating: by managing the symptoms of an unresolved conflict rather than pressing the parties toward settlement, the mission has furnished both sides with a rationale for deferring hard political choices indefinitely.

This critique gains traction in part because of what the mission has demonstrably failed to achieve. Ceasefire violations, though rarely escalating into full-scale engagement, have persisted at a rate that challenges the narrative of stabilisation. Civilian protection mandates, meanwhile, have proved difficult to operationalise in terrain divided by informal but entrenched frontlines. Troop-contributing nations, already stretched by competing commitments, are beginning to question whether open-ended deployments serve broader alliance interests.

What distinguishes the current debate from earlier reviews is its emphasis on structural dysfunction rather than operational shortcomings. Previous assessments tended to recommend procedural fixes — stronger rules of engagement, enhanced intelligence-sharing, revised reporting metrics. The emerging consensus among policy analysts is more fundamental: that the mission's design rests on an assumption of political momentum toward resolution that has never materialised, and that absent a credible political track, continued deployment risks normalising a stalemate that suits neither the affected population nor the stated goals of the intervening community.
readingItems.question: According to the passage, how does the current reassessment differ from earlier reviews of the mission?

options.label: A
options.text: Earlier reviews identified structural design flaws, whereas the current assessment concentrates on improving operational procedures such as rules of engagement.
options.rationale: Incorrect. This directly reverses the contrast drawn in paragraph 3. The passage states that *earlier* reviews focused on procedural fixes, while the *current* debate emphasises structural dysfunction. A reader who processes the paragraph quickly, without tracking the temporal markers 'previous' and 'emerging', is likely to invert the relationship.

options.label: B
options.text: Unlike earlier reviews that focused on procedural remedies, the current debate holds that the mission's difficulties stem from a flawed foundational assumption about political progress.
options.rationale: Correct. Paragraph 3 explicitly contrasts previous recommendations for procedural fixes with the current, more fundamental critique — that the mission's design was premised on political momentum 'that has never materialised'. Option C paraphrases this contrast accurately without reproducing the passage's wording verbatim.

options.label: C
options.text: Unlike earlier reviews, the current reassessment explicitly recommends terminating the mission on the grounds that it has failed to prevent ceasefire violations.
options.rationale: Incorrect. The author never advocates termination; the passage states that continued deployment 'risks normalising a stalemate', which is a cautionary implication, not a policy recommendation. A weak reader may conflate the critical tone with an explicit call for withdrawal, and may also over-weight the mention of ceasefire violations in paragraph 2.

options.label: D
options.text: The current reassessment is driven principally by troop-contributing nations, whereas earlier reviews were conducted by UN policy analysts acting independently of member states.
options.rationale: Incorrect. Although paragraph 2 notes that troop-contributing nations are questioning open-ended deployments, the passage attributes the structural critique to 'policy analysts', not to those nations. This distractor is firmly anchored in the text but misidentifies both the agent behind the current reassessment and the role of earlier reviewers, trapping a reader who correctly recalls the troop-contributing-nation detail but misapplies it.

readingItems.topic: Migration policy and demographic need
readingItems.passage:
Across much of the industrialised world, ageing populations and falling birth rates are placing unprecedented strain on pension systems and healthcare budgets. Demographers have long argued that sustained inward migration offers the most immediate and scalable remedy. Yet the governments most acutely exposed to demographic decline are frequently those that have made the most dramatic promises to curtail immigration — a contradiction that is becoming increasingly difficult to paper over.

The political calculus is not difficult to understand. Voters who associate immigration with wage competition or cultural disruption tend to reward restrictive pledges at the ballot box, particularly in regions where deindustrialisation has sharpened economic insecurity. What is less often acknowledged is the cost of those pledges when they harden into policy: a shrinking working-age population reduces tax revenues, forces up borrowing, and erodes the capacity to fund the social services on which the same ageing electorate depends.

Some governments have attempted to resolve the tension through selective schemes that admit high-skilled migrants while maintaining a posture of restriction on other categories. Critics argue that this approach is both morally incoherent — treating human beings as a commodity to be imported or excluded according to market value — and economically insufficient, since service-sector and care industries, which bear the greatest burden of an ageing society, depend heavily on lower-skilled labour that selective schemes routinely exclude.

The uncomfortable implication is that demographic necessity and restrictive immigration politics are, in the medium term, irreconcilable. Governments that defer that reckoning may find the arithmetic of demography eventually more compelling than any electoral mandate.
readingItems.question: Which of the following best describes the author's implied view of selective high-skilled migration schemes?

options.label: A
options.text: They are an inadequate solution because they exclude the labour most needed in an ageing society.
options.rationale: Key — correctly inferred from the third paragraph. The author presents critics who call selective schemes 'economically insufficient' on the grounds that care and service-sector industries 'depend heavily on lower-skilled labour that selective schemes routinely exclude.' The author offers no rebuttal to this criticism, implying endorsement. The option paraphrases rather than lifts the text: 'inadequate solution' renders 'economically insufficient,' and 'labour most needed' renders the claim about care industries' dependence on lower-skilled workers.

options.label: B
options.text: They are morally defensible provided the number of admitted workers is sufficient.
options.rationale: Distractor — misreversal of the moral argument. The passage explicitly introduces critics who call selective schemes 'morally incoherent'; the author presents no counter-argument to this charge. A reader who notices that moral language appears in the paragraph but inverts its direction — reading the passage as offering a moral defence rather than lodging a moral critique — would be drawn to this option.

options.label: C
options.text: They fail to resolve the underlying tension because they remain too politically unpopular.
options.rationale: Distractor — conflation of two separate arguments. The passage discusses political unpopularity in relation to immigration restriction broadly (paragraph two), not in relation to selective schemes specifically. Selective schemes are introduced as governments' own attempted resolution, not as politically toxic. A reader who blurs the general political argument with the specific paragraph on selective schemes may choose this plausible but unsupported claim.

options.label: D
options.text: They represent the most workable compromise between demographic necessity and voter preferences.
options.rationale: Distractor — the most dangerous option. The passage states that 'some governments have attempted to resolve the tension through selective schemes,' which a weak or hasty reader may interpret as authorial endorsement of selective schemes as a viable middle ground. The critical error is failing to register that the author immediately follows this with unanswered criticisms from both a moral and an economic angle, signalling that the 'attempted resolution' is judged insufficient rather than endorsed.

readingItems.topic: Disinformation and press freedom
readingItems.passage:
The proliferation of state-backed disinformation campaigns has given governments across the democratic world a powerful rhetorical asset: the language of information security. Where earlier administrations might have defended media regulation on grounds of public decency or national cohesion, many now frame restrictions on news organisations and social-media platforms as a necessary defensive posture against foreign manipulation. The shift in justification is not merely semantic. By casting the problem as an external threat rather than a domestic policy choice, legislators insulate themselves from charges of censorship and make it correspondingly harder for critics to mount a principled objection without appearing naïve about the reality of hostile information operations.

The difficulty, of course, is that the same regulatory instruments designed to block foreign propaganda are structurally indistinguishable from those that would silence inconvenient domestic journalism. A law compelling platforms to remove "false or misleading content" necessarily delegates to some authority — governmental, judicial, or corporate — the power to determine what counts as false. That power, once created, does not confine itself neatly to Kremlin-sponsored fabrications. History offers abundant evidence that emergency measures enacted to address genuine crises have a pronounced tendency to outlast the threats that justified them and to find new targets along the way.

Defenders of such legislation argue that the absence of regulation is itself a form of harm: uncontested disinformation distorts public debate and ultimately undermines the democratic conditions that make press freedom meaningful. The argument has merit, yet it conceals a sequencing problem. A democracy that compromises the independence of its press in order to protect democratic debate has not secured debate; it has merely changed the identity of those who control it.
readingItems.question: Which of the following best captures the author's central argument?

options.label: A
options.text: Since foreign disinformation poses only a marginal threat to democratic debate, the regulatory costs of combating it are rarely justified.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — reversal of the author's concession. The author explicitly states in paragraph three that the defenders' argument 'has merit' and that uncontested disinformation 'distorts public debate.' Choosing A requires misreading the author as dismissing the threat altogether, when in fact the author accepts its seriousness before pivoting to the dangers of the proposed remedy.

options.label: B
options.text: The shift toward information-security framing has made it considerably harder for critics to challenge press restrictions on principled grounds.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — supporting point mistaken for the central argument. This observation is accurate and appears in paragraph one, but it describes a rhetorical mechanism that facilitates the problem; it is not the author's conclusion. A candidate who reads too narrowly and stops at paragraph one may elevate this detail to the role of main argument, missing the structural and historical critique that follows.

options.label: C
options.text: Anti-disinformation legislation creates regulatory powers that, once established, are likely to constrain domestic journalism well beyond any immediate foreign-influence threat.
options.rationale: KEY — synthesises the argument across all three paragraphs. Paragraph two establishes that anti-disinformation tools are 'structurally indistinguishable' from censorship instruments and that the power to define falseness 'does not confine itself neatly.' The historical pattern is that emergency measures 'outlast the threats that justified them.' Paragraph three's closing sentence confirms the synthesis: curbing the press to protect democratic debate 'merely changed the identity of those who control it.' This inference is not reproduced verbatim anywhere in the passage.

options.label: D
options.text: Because unchecked disinformation distorts public debate, democratic governments have both the right and the obligation to regulate media content.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — the defenders' view attributed to the author. This represents the position described in paragraph three as belonging to 'defenders of such legislation' — a position the author acknowledges before refuting it with the 'sequencing problem.' A candidate who reads paragraph three uncritically, or who does not recognise the rhetorical move of steel-manning an opposing view before rejecting it, may attribute this conclusion to the author rather than to the interlocutors the author is rebutting.

readingItems.topic: Defence procurement: capability sophistication versus mass and strategic endurance
readingItems.passage:
The argument for acquiring smaller numbers of technologically advanced weapons platforms has long held sway in Western defence ministries. A single fifth-generation combat aircraft, its proponents contend, can accomplish what three or four older jets could not: it is stealthier, more networked, and capable of operating in contested airspace that would be suicidal for legacy platforms. On this reasoning, quality compensates for quantity.

Yet a series of conflicts since 2022 has disturbed this calculus. The war in Ukraine demonstrated that attrition can deplete even well-stocked arsenals at a rate that precision-manufacturing lines struggle to replenish. Missiles expended in a single week of high-intensity operations had taken months, sometimes years, to produce. Some analysts drew a stark conclusion: an armed force optimised for the technically perfect weapon may find itself with nothing to fire after the first fortnight of a peer conflict.

This has prompted a reassessment in several alliance capitals. The debate now turns not on whether advanced capabilities matter — they plainly do — but on the appropriate balance between exquisite, high-unit-cost systems and cheaper, more rapidly producible alternatives. Advocates of the latter argue that a swarm of affordable munitions or drones can saturate adversary defences as effectively as a handful of precision-guided weapons, while preserving mass and strategic endurance.

Critics respond that cheap platforms are more easily countered and may waste themselves against hardened air defences. The disagreement reflects a deeper uncertainty: in the next major conflict, will decisive advantage come from technological superiority at the point of engagement, or from the ability to sustain losses and replenish stocks faster than an adversary?
readingItems.question: What does the passage ultimately present as the core uncertainty shaping the debate it describes?

options.label: A
options.text: Whether alliance governments can sustain the budget commitments required to expand their fleets of fifth-generation aircraft.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — targets a reader who fixates on the cost references in paragraph 3 ('high-unit-cost systems'). The passage never frames the central question as one of fiscal sustainability or whether governments can afford advanced platforms; cost is a variable within the quality-vs.-mass trade-off, not the debate's fundamental uncertainty.

options.label: B
options.text: Whether precision-guided munitions or drone swarms prove more cost-effective against an adversary's hardened air-defence systems.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — targets a reader who treats the specific comparison in paragraphs 3–4 (drones vs. precision munitions against hardened defences) as the passage's main point. This is a sub-argument used to illustrate the broader quality-vs.-mass tension, not the overarching uncertainty the passage poses. The misread elevates a supporting example to the status of the central question.

options.label: C
options.text: Whether the attrition dynamics observed in Ukraine are applicable to a high-intensity war between technologically matched competitors.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — targets a reader who treats Ukraine — the most prominent concrete example — as the debate's primary focus. The Ukraine conflict is invoked to demonstrate how attrition can invalidate the quality-over-quantity assumption, but the passage's scope is broader: it asks what determines decisive advantage in any future peer conflict, not specifically whether Ukraine provides a valid template.

options.label: D
options.text: Whether decisive advantage in conflict derives from platform sophistication or from strategic resilience and industrial replenishment capacity.
options.rationale: KEY — paraphrases the closing rhetorical question without lifting it verbatim: 'technological superiority at the point of engagement' becomes 'platform sophistication', and 'the ability to sustain losses and replenish stocks faster than an adversary' becomes 'strategic resilience and industrial replenishment capacity'. This synthesis captures the argument's architecture across all four paragraphs and requires the reader to follow the passage's reasoning rather than scan for a matching phrase.

readingItems.topic: Climate-Driven Arctic Resource Competition
readingItems.passage:
The accelerating retreat of Arctic sea ice has recast the region from a remote wilderness into a contested economic frontier, exposing a deep rift between states that treat the newfound access as a sovereign windfall and international bodies that argue for collective stewardship. Russia and Canada have invested heavily in icebreaker capacity and extended continental shelf claims, positioning themselves to control emerging shipping corridors and exploit offshore hydrocarbon and mineral deposits that have become accessible only as permafrost and sea ice recede. Their position rests on established maritime law, which awards exclusive economic zones to coastal states regardless of how those zones came to be navigable.

Critics, however, contend that climate-driven resource access represents a fundamentally different case. Because the opening of the Arctic is the direct consequence of a global atmospheric failure — caused overwhelmingly by industrial emissions from states far removed from the region — the resulting resource windfall should not accrue exclusively to those fortunate enough to hold adjacent coastlines. Small island states, whose own territories face submersion precisely because of the same warming, have pressed at international forums for a share in Arctic governance and revenues, a demand that Arctic-rim powers have resisted with little ambiguity.

The disagreement crystallises a broader tension that climate change is forcing into the open: whether the redistribution of natural resources caused by environmental disruption is a matter of geopolitical realpolitik or of distributive justice. So far, the architecture of international law has offered little resolution, and the window for negotiated settlement may narrow as commercial exploitation gathers pace.
readingItems.question: What does the passage imply about the position taken by Arctic-rim powers in this dispute?

options.label: A
options.text: They have signalled readiness to negotiate a governance framework that includes non-Arctic states.
options.rationale: Distractor — contradicted by the text. The passage explicitly states that Arctic-rim powers have 'resisted with little ambiguity' the demands of small island states for a share in governance. A weak reader may conflate the mention of 'international forums' with a willingness on the part of Arctic states to negotiate, missing the unambiguous signal of resistance.

options.label: B
options.text: They invoke established legal norms to defend claims whose origins may be considered inequitable.
options.rationale: Key. The passage states that Arctic-rim states ground their claims in 'established maritime law' (established legal norms). The reader must then synthesise this with the critics' argument in the second paragraph — that the opening of the Arctic is the product of a global atmospheric failure, rendering such claims potentially inequitable in origin. That inference is implied but never directly stated; neither paragraph alone yields the answer, so pattern-matching the wording is insufficient.

options.label: C
options.text: They argue that their infrastructure investments confer a prior right to newly accessible resources.
options.rationale: Distractor — misread. The passage notes that Russia and Canada have 'invested heavily in icebreaker capacity,' which a superficial reader may take as the stated basis of their claim. The text, however, presents these investments as strategic positioning moves, not as legal justification; the explicit legal foundation given is established maritime law, not capital expenditure.

options.label: D
options.text: They contend that existing international law is ill-suited to adjudicating climate-driven disputes.
options.rationale: Distractor — reversal. Arctic-rim states actively deploy international law in their favour, invoking maritime conventions and continental shelf regimes. The passage implies they find existing law convenient, not inadequate. A weak reader may over-generalise from the final paragraph's observation that 'the architecture of international law has offered little resolution,' misattributing that critique to the Arctic-rim powers rather than to the author.

readingItems.topic: Reshoring politics versus industrial concentration risk
readingItems.passage:
The push to reshore manufacturing has been framed, in most Western capitals, as a straightforward national-security imperative. Concentrated production in a single jurisdiction — most pointedly, China's dominance of semiconductor packaging, rare-earth refining, and pharmaceutical precursors — was held to have created unacceptable strategic vulnerabilities, exposed most vividly during the pandemic. Yet the case is less tidy than its advocates suggest.

Efficiency and resilience are not merely different points on a single spectrum; they are often genuinely incompatible. Lean supply chains are lean precisely because they exploit the comparative advantages of geographically dispersed production and hold minimal buffer stock. Rebuilding those chains domestically or within a ring of trusted allies delivers redundancy but at a cost: higher unit costs, idle over-capacity in quiet periods, and a replication of capabilities that may sit underutilised for years. The International Monetary Fund has estimated that deep fragmentation of global trade could reduce world output by as much as seven per cent over the long run — a figure that falls disproportionately on smaller, trade-dependent economies.

What is rarely acknowledged in reshoring advocacy is who absorbs those costs. Subsidies for domestic semiconductor fabs or battery plants transfer the bill from the consumer to the taxpayer, but the bill remains. Meanwhile, the friend-shoring logic — concentrating suppliers within a politically aligned bloc rather than returning them home — does little to reduce technical concentration risk unless allies themselves diversify their capabilities. A supply chain that once ran from Guangdong to Rotterdam and now runs from Guadalajara to Rotterdam is geopolitically tidier but industrially similar in its single-point vulnerabilities.
readingItems.question: Which statement best captures the author's central contention about supply-chain reshoring?

options.label: A
options.text: Reshoring and friend-shoring are politically motivated responses that leave the core problem of industrial concentration largely unresolved.
options.rationale: CORRECT. The key synthesises the passage's overall argument. The political framing is signalled in paragraph one ('framed... as a national-security imperative') and the friend-shoring critique appears in paragraph three ('geopolitically tidier but industrially similar in its single-point vulnerabilities'). No single sentence states this conclusion; the reader must infer across all three paragraphs.

options.label: B
options.text: The economic penalties of supply-chain fragmentation fall most heavily on trade-dependent developing nations.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — true-but-not-the-main-argument. The IMF statistic about smaller economies appears in paragraph two as a supporting detail illustrating the cost of fragmentation, not as the author's central contention. A weak reader who fixates on this memorable figure may mistake a supporting point for the thesis.

options.label: C
options.text: Lean supply chains created the conditions for pandemic-era shortages and must give way to domestic production models.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — reversal of the author's stance. The pandemic is cited as an example of exposed vulnerability, not as a case for domestic production. The author explicitly challenges the reshoring argument ('the case is less tidy than its advocates suggest'), so reading the passage as an endorsement of reshoring inverts its direction of argument.

options.label: D
options.text: Subsidising domestic semiconductor and battery manufacturing is a more effective risk-reduction policy than relocating suppliers to allied nations.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — reversal of implied judgement. The passage notes that subsidies 'transfer the bill from the consumer to the taxpayer, but the bill remains', casting doubt on subsidies as a genuine solution. The author presents both subsidies and friend-shoring as inadequate, not one as superior to the other. A candidate reading the subsidy sentence in isolation may infer a comparative endorsement the text does not support.

readingItems.topic: Space governance: the strategic-dependency paradox
readingItems.passage:
The congestion now defining low Earth orbit presents a governance paradox that the international community has so far failed to resolve. Thousands of active satellites share an increasingly crowded band of orbital space with tens of thousands of tracked debris objects; yet the foundational treaty governing conduct in space — the 1967 Outer Space Treaty — was drafted when orbital activity was the preserve of two superpowers and makes no provision for the commercial operators, the mega-constellations, or the anti-satellite weapons that now define the environment.

Efforts to update the framework have consistently foundered on a structural tension. Space-faring states acknowledge, at least rhetorically, the shared interest in keeping the orbital commons usable; voluntary codes of conduct, debris-mitigation guidelines, and norm-building exercises have accordingly proliferated. Yet no state has proved willing to accept binding constraints on kinetic anti-satellite capabilities, because each views the satellite networks of its adversaries as legitimate targets in any future conflict. The voluntary approach, in this sense, reproduces the problem it was meant to solve: norms without enforcement do nothing to deter a state that calculates the military gain from an anti-satellite strike to outweigh the reputational cost of violating a guideline.

There is a further asymmetry that complicates any legal solution. The leading space powers have the most to lose from orbital debris — their commercial and military dependencies on satellite infrastructure are the deepest — but they also have the greatest incentive to preserve an anti-satellite option as leverage. Smaller spacefaring states, by contrast, have less infrastructure to protect and correspondingly less reason to limit capabilities they have only recently acquired. This divergence of interests means that any treaty stringent enough to address the underlying problem would require the states most resistant to signing it.

**The passage implies that binding international rules on anti-satellite weapons are difficult to achieve primarily because**

options.label: A
options.text: voluntary codes of conduct have already prevented the worst forms of orbital congestion, reducing political pressure for a legal framework.
options.rationale: Distractor — reverses the passage's argument. The text states that voluntary norms 'reproduce the problem' rather than solve it; a weak reader who focuses on 'proliferated' in paragraph 2 may infer the norms have been effective.

options.label: B
options.text: the structural limitations of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty make it legally impossible to extend international regulation to anti-satellite capabilities.
options.rationale: Distractor — conflates the passage's mention of the treaty's outdated scope with the actual obstacle identified. The 1967 treaty is cited to illustrate the gap between the existing framework and current realities, not to argue that the treaty itself blocks further law-making.

options.label: C
options.text: the states most dependent on satellite infrastructure also have the strongest strategic incentive to preserve anti-satellite options, making them resistant to stringent constraints.
options.rationale: Key — synthesises paragraphs 2 and 3. The passage states explicitly that leading space powers have 'the greatest incentive to preserve an anti-satellite option as leverage' and concludes that any sufficiently stringent treaty 'would require the states most resistant to signing it.' This paraphrases and infers rather than lifting the text verbatim.

options.label: D
options.text: smaller spacefaring nations refuse to engage in treaty negotiations, perceiving the process as structured to protect the interests of established space powers.
options.rationale: Distractor — introduces an outside assumption not supported by the text. The passage attributes smaller states' reluctance to a divergence of material interests (they have less infrastructure to protect and less reason to limit capabilities), not to procedural grievances about the negotiation process.

readingItems.topic: Boom-and-bust funding cycles and the erosion of institutional trust in pandemic preparedness
readingItems.passage:
The institutional memory of public-health systems is shorter than the pathogens they are designed to contain. Each major outbreak — SARS in 2003, H1N1 in 2009, Ebola in 2014 — generated political momentum for investment in surge capacity, stockpiling, and early-warning infrastructure. Yet in each case, as mortality figures fell and media attention drifted, legislatures quietly trimmed the budgets of the agencies responsible for maintaining that preparedness. By 2019, several high-income countries that had ranked near the top of global health-security indices had quietly hollowed out the laboratory networks and reserve stockpiles their own assessments had identified as critical.

This pattern does more than leave systems materially underprepared. It corrodes the credibility of the warning apparatus itself. Officials who sound the alarm before a pathogen reaches epidemic scale must rely on institutional authority that sustained underfunding has already damaged. When governments dismantle the very infrastructure they have publicly lauded, citizens internalize that preparedness is performative — a response to perceived crisis rather than a durable commitment. The erosion of institutional trust that followed in 2020 was therefore not simply a communications failure; it was the predictable consequence of a policy cycle that treats preparedness as discretionary spending.

Whether any remedy exists within existing fiscal frameworks is debatable. Hypothecated pandemic funds — ring-fenced budgets insulated from annual appropriations — have been proposed by several international commissions, but they require the same legislative will that the boom-and-bust cycle demonstrates is scarce. The deeper problem may be structural: democratic polities optimize for visible, immediate threats, while pandemic preparedness demands investment in contingencies that, if successful, remain invisible.
readingItems.question: What does the author imply was the primary cause of the erosion of public trust in health institutions that emerged in 2020?

options.label: A
options.text: Governments consistently failed to communicate early-warning assessments in ways that citizens could understand and trust
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — misread of the explicit rebuttal. The author acknowledges a communications dimension but immediately dismisses it as the root cause: 'not simply a communications failure.' A careless reader who stops at this phrase without absorbing the contrastive clause may treat the rejected explanation as the accepted one.

options.label: B
options.text: Wealthy nations structurally prioritized visible economic pressures over health-security investment in the years following each major outbreak
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — over-generalisation with unsupported motive. The text records that legislatures trimmed preparedness budgets as threats receded, but it does not state that economic competitiveness was the driving motive, nor does it frame the cuts as a deliberate structural prioritization of the economy. The phrase 'in the years following each major outbreak' also reverses the temporal logic: cuts came as attention drifted, not consistently in the years after.

options.label: C
options.text: Global health-security indices proved to be unreliable predictors of a country's actual capacity to respond to a pandemic
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR — true-but-irrelevant. The text does imply that high index rankings did not prevent hollowing-out, which a reader might re-cast as index unreliability. However, the author's argument concerns what the funding cycle communicated to citizens, not whether the indices were methodologically sound. Selecting this option mistakes a textual detail (rankings vs. real capacity) for the author's central claim about trust erosion.

options.label: D
options.text: A recurring cycle of post-outbreak investment followed by budget cuts signalled to citizens that preparedness was a political gesture rather than a lasting commitment
options.rationale: KEY — synthesises the boom-and-bust pattern (paragraphs 1–2) with the author's explicit causal claim ('predictable consequence of a policy cycle') and the analytical inference that citizens 'internalize that preparedness is performative — a response to perceived crisis rather than a durable commitment.' No single sentence states this; the reader must combine the documented pattern, the mechanism of public inference, and the author's causal conclusion.

readingItems.topic: Alliance burden-sharing trade-offs
readingItems.passage:
The arithmetic of collective defence is rarely as clean as its architects suggest. When the more powerful members of an alliance absorb a disproportionate share of its costs — garrisoning troops abroad, maintaining ready forces at scale, funding shared infrastructure — they do not simply subsidise the security of smaller partners. They also accumulate a form of structural influence that no treaty clause can explicitly confer: the implicit veto that accrues to indispensability. The partner that pays the bills sets, however informally, the agenda.

Yet the demand for burden-sharing rebalancing, which has recurred with particular intensity since the 2008 financial crisis, carries its own quiet contradiction. States that raise their defence expenditure to satisfy alliance benchmarks do not thereby become more deferential; they tend, on the contrary, to become considerably less so. A defence ministry that can point to a credible national capability finds it easier to dissent from the leading power's preferred course of action. Burden-sharing, in other words, tends to democratise the alliance even as it distributes costs more equitably. The leading power may ultimately find that it has paid, with some precision, for its own diminished authority.

This is not an argument for the perpetuation of asymmetry — the resentments it breeds on both sides are real enough. The subsidising power tires of its role and says so; the subsidised power chafes at dependence and bristles at the condescension that tends to accompany it. The question is whether alliance managers have been candid about the full terms of the bargain: that correcting a fiscal imbalance is also, unavoidably, a reallocation of political weight. Fiscal equity and political hierarchy are, it seems, harder to sustain simultaneously than either the paymasters or the free-riders have been willing to concede.
readingItems.question: What is the primary rhetorical function of the opening statement of the third paragraph — "This is not an argument for the perpetuation of asymmetry"?

options.label: A
options.text: To signal that the author, having outlined the leading power's dilemma, is now redirecting analytical sympathy toward the grievances of smaller alliance members.
options.rationale: Distractor. The third paragraph does enumerate smaller members' resentment of dependence and condescension, and a shallow reader moving from para 2 (the leading power's loss of authority) to para 3 (smaller powers' chafing) may interpret the shift in subject as a shift in authorial sympathy. In fact the paragraph's purpose is not to champion a different party but to pre-empt a misreading of the preceding argument.

options.label: B
options.text: To forestall the inference that the preceding paragraph's argument constitutes a defence of continued fiscal dependence within the alliance.
options.rationale: Key. Paragraph two demonstrates that successful burden-sharing rebalancing erodes the leading power's structural influence, a line of reasoning that could be misread as an implicit endorsement of asymmetry (since asymmetry preserves that influence). The disclaimer explicitly closes off that misreading, clarifying that the author is not advocating the status quo but insisting on intellectual honesty about the full political consequences of rebalancing.

options.label: C
options.text: To assert that the political costs of sustaining asymmetric burden-sharing ultimately outweigh those of pressing for rapid fiscal rebalancing.
options.rationale: Distractor. The paragraph does state that asymmetry's resentments are 'real enough,' and a reader focused on that enumeration may infer that the author is implicitly ranking costs and concluding that asymmetry is the greater harm. The text makes no such comparative claim, however; the resentments on both sides are noted precisely to establish that neither arrangement is painless, not to adjudicate between them.

options.label: D
options.text: To acknowledge that the resentments generated by fiscal dependence are as strategically significant as the structural leverage the leading power derives from it.
options.rationale: Distractor. Because the paragraph discusses both the subsidising power's fatigue and the subsidised power's chafing, a superficial reader may conclude that the disclaimer is setting up a symmetrical treatment of both parties' grievances. The passage's actual intent at this point is not analytical balance between perspectives but a rhetorical pre-emption of the misreading that para 2 defends asymmetry.

readingItems.topic: The contested effectiveness of economic sanctions
readingItems.passage:
The literature on economic sanctions has long been riven by a paradox that its practitioners seldom acknowledge. Those who impose sanctions routinely cite their eventual success — the dismantling of apartheid, the Iranian nuclear accord, the arms embargo on Liberia — as proof of a coercive tool with genuine bite. Their critics point with equal facility to the decades-long siege of Cuba, the perpetuation of North Korea's nuclear programme, and Russia's relative equanimity under successive rounds of Western restrictions. Both camps, it turns out, are selecting from the same body of evidence; they simply impose different definitions of what a sanction is supposed to achieve.

The most rigorous attempt to settle the matter, the Hufbauer-Schott-Elliott dataset that has shaped the field since its first edition in 1985, concluded that sanctions "succeed" in roughly one-third of cases. Critics of the dataset subsequently argued that the methodology was biased toward confirming effectiveness, since researchers retrospectively coded cases as successes whenever a targeted government made any concession, however peripheral to the original demand. Revised analyses halved the success rate. Defenders of the original findings replied that revised analyses introduced their own distortions by applying an impossibly narrow definition of success — the complete and verifiable capitulation of the target — that no diplomatic instrument, including military force, could regularly satisfy.

What neither side has been fully prepared to concede is that the framing of the debate may be the problem. Sanctions are rarely deployed in the expectation that they will, by themselves, compel a government to alter fundamental policy. They are deployed to demonstrate resolve, to satisfy domestic audiences, to placate allies who resist more costly options, and to mark a moral threshold — a function closer to public ritual than to strategic coercion. To evaluate them exclusively against the benchmark of behavioural change is to take seriously a rationale that their architects often advance in bad faith.
readingItems.question: Which of the following best captures the author's central implicit claim?

options.label: A
options.text: The empirical record on sanctions is too sparse and methodologically contested for any general theory of their effectiveness to be credible.
options.rationale: Distractor targeting readers who treat paragraph 2 as the heart of the argument. The methodological dispute between the Hufbauer-Schott-Elliott camp and its critics is real and detailed, and a reader who stalls there may conclude that the author's point is simply that the evidence base is irredeemably contested. But the author does not argue that better data would resolve the question; the final paragraph explicitly frames the entire evidentiary debate as a category error — asking the wrong question of the evidence altogether. This option mistakes one analytical episode for the author's ultimate argument.

options.label: B
options.text: Sanctions would achieve more of their stated aims if policymakers were candid about pursuing political legitimacy rather than behavioural compliance.
options.rationale: Distractor targeting readers who over-infer a prescriptive recommendation from the author's diagnostic final paragraph. The passage establishes that sanctions serve performative and political functions; a careful but slightly over-reaching reader might take this as implying that explicit acknowledgement of those functions would improve outcomes. The author, however, makes no such claim — the conclusion is diagnostic and implicitly ironic, not advisory. This option introduces a normative prescription that goes meaningfully beyond what the text supports.

options.label: C
options.text: The prevailing debate about sanctions mistakes the instrument's primary political function for the strategic purpose its proponents officially claim.
options.rationale: KEY. The author constructs the argument across all three paragraphs: both pro-sanctions and anti-sanctions scholars argue about behavioural effectiveness (strategic coercion), yet the architects of sanctions know the real function is performative — demonstrating resolve, managing allies, satisfying domestic audiences, marking a moral threshold — and argue the strategic-coercion rationale 'in bad faith.' Synthesising these elements yields the conclusion that the dominant evaluative framework confuses the instrument's actual political function with its stated strategic purpose. The word 'prevailing' correctly encompasses both camps of the debate, which the author critiques symmetrically.

options.label: D
options.text: Governments that impose sanctions are chiefly motivated by domestic political pressures rather than by any coherent strategic objective.
options.rationale: Distractor targeting readers who skim paragraph 3 and fix on the mention of domestic audiences and risk-averse allies as motivations. The author does list domestic politics among the real drivers, making this option superficially plausible. However, the author enumerates multiple distinct motivations (resolve, alliance management, moral signalling) without ranking them, and the central argument is not about which motivation dominates but about the structural mismatch between the stated purpose and the actual function. A reader who misreads the list as a hierarchy, and drops the 'bad faith' framing of the final sentence, is likely to select this option.

readingItems.topic: Energy transition and security of supply
readingItems.passage:
The green transition has been marketed, with some justice, as an escape from geopolitical vulnerability. Replacing imported hydrocarbons with domestically generated wind and solar electricity, the argument runs, liberates energy policy from the caprices of autocratic exporters and the volatility of commodity markets. It is an appealing narrative, and not an entirely mistaken one. Yet the closer one examines the supply chains underpinning the transition, the more the rhetoric of emancipation begins to resemble a change of dependency rather than its abolition.

The minerals required for batteries, electrolysers, and photovoltaic panels — lithium, cobalt, nickel, rare earths — are concentrated in a handful of countries, several of which present their own political risks. China refines approximately eighty per cent of the world's rare earths and dominates the processing of most critical battery metals, while the Democratic Republic of Congo supplies more than half of global cobalt output under conditions of chronic instability. Europe and North America, having largely divested from the extraction and processing of these materials over the preceding decades, are now attempting to reconstruct supply chains from a near-standing start.

The urgency of climate targets has meanwhile imposed a logic that militates against patience. Governments under pressure to demonstrate decarbonisation progress have accelerated renewable deployment while deferring the harder question of what happens at scale when the wind does not blow and the sun does not shine. Storage technology remains expensive; interconnection grids are politically contentious; and gas — the pragmatist's bridge fuel — carries the ideological taint of the fossil era. The result is a policy landscape in which transition and security are pursued simultaneously but not always coherently, a condition that one energy minister, with apparent self-awareness, recently described as "building the plane while arguing about the runway."
readingItems.question: In the final paragraph, what does the author primarily achieve by citing the energy minister's remark about "building the plane while arguing about the runway"?

options.label: A
options.text: The author demonstrates that the practical obstacles to grid-scale storage are already on the radar of energy ministries.
options.rationale: A reader who focuses on the literal vehicle of the metaphor — a plane being built in flight — may infer the author is simply noting that engineering difficulties are widely recognised. This misreads the rhetorical function: the quote is deployed to validate the author's thesis about structural policy incoherence, not to catalogue specific technical shortcomings of which officials are aware.

options.label: B
options.text: The author concedes that policymakers retain a clear strategic direction even when specific implementation choices remain contested.
options.rationale: This inverts the implication. The minister's metaphor connotes confusion and unresolved contradiction, not the possession of a clear overarching vision. A reader who interprets 'apparent self-awareness' as evidence of strategic competence — awareness of one's goals — rather than of acknowledged self-contradiction will be drawn to this option, reversing the passage's logic.

options.label: C
options.text: The author suggests that ideological pressure to decarbonise has become a more significant obstacle to coherent policy than technological unreadiness.
options.rationale: The passage does invoke 'ideological taint' in reference to gas and notes that governments driven by climate-target pressure have rushed deployment, both of which could tempt a reader to conclude that the minister's quote foregrounds ideology as the singular barrier. However, the metaphor is offered as a capsule description of incoherence in general — the plane and the runway being addressed simultaneously without coordination — rather than as a verdict that ideology outweighs technology as an obstacle. Choosing D requires privileging one clause in the preceding sentences over the broader rhetorical function of the quotation.

options.label: D
options.text: The author implies that the structural incoherence he diagnoses is effectively conceded by those who design energy policy.
options.rationale: CORRECT KEY. The minister's remark is introduced with the carefully chosen qualifier 'apparent self-awareness,' signalling that the policymaker implicitly acknowledges the contradiction the author has spent the passage constructing: transition and security are being pursued 'simultaneously but not always coherently.' The quote thereby transforms an external analytical critique into an admission from within the apparatus itself, reinforcing the argument that incoherence is a recognised condition, not merely an observer's inference.

readingItems.topic: Geopolitics & Security Policy — Deterrence Doctrine
readingItems.passage:
The vocabulary of deterrence has always been peculiarly resistant to obsolescence. During the Cold War, strategists invested enormous intellectual energy in a framework premised on two propositions: that states are rational actors willing and able to calculate costs against gains, and that the threat of catastrophic punishment will reliably prevent aggression. What is striking, in retrospect, is how rarely this framework was subjected to serious empirical scrutiny even as its architects acknowledged, in private, that it rested on assumptions no game theorist would endorse without considerable qualification.

The shift now underway in Western capitals goes under the label "integrated deterrence" — a concept that, in its more candid articulations, amounts to an admission that the old architecture has been rendered anachronistic by a convergence of pressures: the proliferation of capable but opaque state actors, the erosion of escalation ladders that once provided strategic grammar, and the emergence of domains — cyber, space, cognitive — in which the logic of punishment is genuinely difficult to operationalise.

Proponents argue that integration — of conventional, nuclear, cyber and economic instruments across alliances — restores the credibility that single-domain postures have forfeited. Critics, not unreasonably, detect in the new vocabulary an attempt to disguise strategic uncertainty behind taxonomic novelty. The honest position, rarely articulated in official documents, is that deterrence theory is being rebuilt in real time, under operational pressure, with no guarantee that adversaries are reading from the same conceptual script.

Whether this constitutes progress depends entirely on what one thought deterrence was ever doing. If it was always less a theory than a rhetorical technology for managing domestic and alliance anxieties — a point the historical record does not entirely refute — then the shift to integrated deterrence may be less a revolution than a renovation, papering over foundations whose load-bearing capacity has never been independently verified.
readingItems.question: What does the author's characterization of deterrence as a "rhetorical technology" imply about the shift to integrated deterrence?

options.label: A
options.text: The new framework is likely to serve the same stabilising fiction as its predecessor, leaving the unverified foundations of deterrence theory intact.
options.rationale: Correct. 'Rhetorical technology for managing domestic and alliance anxieties' identifies deterrence as a discursive instrument rather than a verified strategic mechanism. The conditional structure of the final paragraph — 'If it was always less a theory than a rhetorical technology... then the shift... may be less a revolution than a renovation' — explicitly extends this diagnosis to integrated deterrence. The key requires the reader to track the author's implication across the conditional and to synthesise 'papering over' with 'load-bearing capacity has never been independently verified' into a coherent judgement about the new framework's continuity with the old.

options.label: B
options.text: Integrated deterrence has at last discarded the rhetorical trappings of its Cold War predecessor in favour of empirically testable strategic propositions.
options.rationale: Reversal distractor. The passage's final paragraph states that the shift may be 'less a revolution than a renovation, papering over foundations whose load-bearing capacity has never been independently verified.' A candidate who focuses narrowly on the proponents' argument in paragraph three and fails to register the author's skeptical framing in paragraph four will find this option superficially attractive, mistaking the absence of explicit condemnation for endorsement.

options.label: C
options.text: The term reveals a fundamental dishonesty in Cold War strategy that present-day policymakers have corrected by adopting a more transparent and accountable framework.
options.rationale: Misread distractor. The passage does not suggest that current policymakers have corrected the problem. On the contrary, 'rarely articulated in official documents' and 'papering over' signal continued concealment rather than greater transparency. A candidate who reads 'rhetorical technology' as a purely historical critique and does not track the author's extension of that critique into the present — particularly through the conditional in the final paragraph — will find this option plausible.

options.label: D
options.text: The new concept gains genuine credibility because adversaries now share the same calculus as its architects, a condition Cold War deterrence never achieved.
options.rationale: Reversal distractor. The passage explicitly warns that deterrence theory is being rebuilt 'with no guarantee that adversaries are reading from the same conceptual script.' Option D inverts this by claiming the shared-calculus condition has now been satisfied. A candidate who recalls the rational-actor premise from paragraph one but misattributes its resolution to integrated deterrence, rather than recognising it as an enduring and unresolved problem, will find this option plausible.

readingItems.topic: Security & Defence Policy — Conscription vs. Professional Forces
readingItems.passage:
The return of conscription to European policy debates has been greeted with a curious mixture of martial nostalgia and strategic pragmatism, neither of which survives close scrutiny. Advocates point to Finland and Norway — states that have retained compulsory service throughout the post-Cold War interlude — as proof that the citizen-soldier model remains viable in the age of networked warfare. Yet the comparison is selectively applied. Both Nordic cases involve societies with exceptionally high civic trust, small populations, and long traditions of integrating conscripts into a coherent national defence culture. Transplanting the model to larger, more socially fragmented polities risks producing large numbers of underequipped, undertrained personnel whose presence inflates order-of-battle statistics without meaningfully enhancing combat power.

The professional-force lobby is scarcely more candid. Its preferred arguments — that volunteer armies are more effective, more adaptable, and cheaper per capability unit — carry genuine weight in peacetime conditions but tend to dissolve under prolonged attrition, as the war in Ukraine has demonstrated with uncomfortable clarity. A professional force small enough to be fiscally defensible may also prove too small to absorb casualties at the rate a peer conflict demands.

What neither side has been willing to say plainly is that the case for conscription rests, in the end, not on military effectiveness at all, but on a political theory: that a democracy which delegates its defence entirely to a professional caste gradually loses both the willingness and the institutional capacity to sustain a war whose costs are felt only by a narrow stratum of society. Whether or not conscript armies fight better, the argument runs, they distribute the burden — and, with it, the political accountability — more equitably. That this argument is rarely made in the open, preferring instead to dress itself in the language of readiness and deterrence, tells us something about the limits of what contemporary political culture is prepared to say aloud.
readingItems.question: What does the author imply by observing that the real case for conscription "prefers to dress itself in the language of readiness and deterrence"?

options.label: A
options.text: Conscription advocates knowingly misrepresent their motives, substituting palatable military arguments for the political reasoning they privately consider more compelling.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR. This traps readers who interpret 'dress itself' as evidence of deliberate deception by individual advocates. The author, however, attributes the reframing not to bad faith but to a structural cultural inhibition: 'the limits of what contemporary political culture is prepared to say aloud.' The word 'knowingly' in this option introduces intentionality that the text does not support, but the distinction is fine enough to mislead any reader who has not fully absorbed the final sentence's framing.

options.label: B
options.text: The substantive argument for conscription is a political one about democratic burden-sharing, but it is recast in military-technical terms because political culture is unwilling to articulate it openly.
options.rationale: KEY. The author explicitly states that the case for conscription rests 'not on military effectiveness at all, but on a political theory' of equitable burden distribution. The final sentence then identifies why this argument goes unstated — 'the limits of what contemporary political culture is prepared to say aloud' — and notes that the argument instead 'dress[es] itself in the language of readiness and deterrence.' This option synthesises both observations without importing any element from outside the text.

options.label: C
options.text: Military-effectiveness arguments for conscription are ultimately stronger than political ones, which explains why they feature more prominently in public advocacy for compulsory service.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR. This directly reverses the author's explicit claim. The passage states that the real case rests 'not on military effectiveness at all, but on a political theory,' and paragraph one actively undermines the military-effectiveness argument by questioning the Nordic comparison. A reader who processes the text superficially — noting that military language dominates the public debate without registering the author's ironic inversion — may conclude that its prominence reflects its strength rather than a strategic evasion.

options.label: D
options.text: Professional military establishments have deliberately marginalised the democratic-legitimacy argument in order to protect their own institutional standing and ensure the volunteer-force model prevails.
options.rationale: DISTRACTOR. This option introduces a causal agent (professional military establishments acting in self-interest) and a mechanism (deliberate suppression) that are absent from the passage. The text attributes the silence to 'political culture' as a diffuse social phenomenon, not to institutional lobbying. A hasty reader may conflate the 'professional-force lobby' mentioned in paragraph two — criticised there for its own lack of candour — with an active effort to suppress a rival argument, producing a plausible but unwarranted inference.

readingItems.topic: Disputed interpretations of inflation statistics
readingItems.passage:
The same set of numbers, it turns out, can be read as a vindication or a warning, depending on who is doing the reading. When the statistical office released its quarterly inflation figures last spring — a headline rate of 3.1 per cent, down from a peak of 8.7 — the government's communications apparatus moved with practised efficiency. Ministers spoke of a "decisive turning point." The central bank's governor, never one to resist a well-turned phrase, described the trajectory as "gratifying." Editorialists sympathetic to the administration wrote of a soft landing achieved.

Economists in the opposing camp arrived at the same data by a different route and emerged with an altogether different destination in mind. They noted that the headline rate masked a core figure stripped of energy and food prices that had barely moved; that real wages, after adjusting for the cumulative price level rather than the rate of change, remained some seven per cent below their pre-shock values; and that the apparent deceleration owed more to base effects — the mechanical consequence of comparing against a period of already-elevated prices — than to any durable improvement in underlying conditions. They were less interested in the rate of change of the rate of change than in what a loaf of bread actually cost.

Both camps, in other words, were looking at the same mountain from opposite slopes and describing entirely different terrain. The dispute was not, strictly speaking, about the data. It was about which data point deserved to be called "inflation" — the headline figure that fills front pages, or the accumulated price level that fills shopping baskets. That governments have tended to prefer the former and households the latter is, perhaps, not a coincidence.
readingItems.question: What is the author implying with the closing observation that the respective preferences governments and households show for different measures of inflation are "perhaps, not a coincidence"?

options.label: A
options.text: The contested readings stem from a genuine methodological ambiguity in macroeconomic statistics, and the author regards both the government's and the critics' interpretations as equally defensible on technical grounds.
options.rationale: Distractor targeting readers who focus on the technical detail in paragraph 2 (core rates, base effects, real wages adjustment). The passage presents those details as arguments the critics advance, not as evidence that measurement is symmetrically broken or that both sides stand on equal analytical footing. The author's ironic understatement in the final sentence signals a clear, if restrained, judgment — not an agnostic shrug about methodology.

options.label: B
options.text: The author presents governments and critics as selecting their preferred metric in good faith, each reflecting a legitimate economic reality, and treats the dispute as one that the data alone cannot adjudicate.
options.rationale: Distractor targeting readers who mistake the passage's evenhanded narrative structure for authorial neutrality. The passage does give both camps space to make their case, but 'not a coincidence' injects a pointed, sardonic judgment: the preference is not analytically motivated but politically convenient. The author does not ultimately hold the dispute to be irresolvable or both positions to be in equally good faith.

options.label: C
options.text: Governments gravitate toward the headline rate because its declining trajectory suits their political interests better than the stagnant picture conveyed by accumulated price levels, and the author treats this tendency as predictable rather than neutral.
options.rationale: Correct key. The phrase 'not a coincidence' is an ironic understatement: the author implies that the preference is explained by self-interest, not by analytical superiority. This reading is prepared by the sardonic inventory of favourable rhetoric in paragraph 1 ('practised efficiency,' 'well-turned phrase,' 'decisive turning point') and the contrast with the critics' grounded, lived-cost framing in paragraph 2. The key paraphrases the implied judgment without lifting any phrase verbatim.

options.label: D
options.text: The author sides with the critics by identifying base effects as the decisive factor in the dispute, implying that the apparent deceleration in inflation is a statistical artefact that should settle the debate in the critics' favour.
options.rationale: Distractor targeting readers who concentrate on the technical argument in paragraph 2 and infer that the author is endorsing the critics' methodology outright. While the author clearly has more sympathy with the picture of lived costs, the closing sentence concerns the politically motivated choice of preferred metric, not a verdict on which measure is technically correct. The author does not declare base effects decisive or conclude that the critics win the analytical argument.

readingItems.topic: AI governance and dual-use technology
readingItems.passage:
The architecture of international AI governance has, in the space of a few years, accumulated the institutional trappings of maturity — safety boards, export-control schedules, multilateral communiqués — without acquiring the substance those trappings are meant to represent. Nowhere is this gap more apparent than in the treatment of dual-use AI systems, where the line between a civilian foundation model and a tool for autonomous targeting or biological design assistance is less a bright boundary than a design choice made after the fact.

What is striking is not the absence of regulatory effort but its peculiar character. Governments have learned to speak the language of responsible development with remarkable fluency — publishing frontier-AI safety frameworks, commissioning red-team exercises, and convening summits at the kinds of country houses that historically hosted arms-limitation talks. The ceremonial resemblance to arms control is presumably not accidental, yet it obscures a crucial dissimilarity: the old treaties addressed systems whose lethality was their defining feature, whereas the capabilities now being managed were engineered primarily for commerce and only subsequently discovered to be militarily consequential. The governance instruments designed for one category are being retrofitted, imperfectly, to the other.

The resulting regime is one in which compliance signals virtue without constraining capability. States that publish safety frameworks can, in the same administrative season, approve export waivers for the very model families those frameworks purport to restrict. Companies that submit to voluntary commitments retain the discretion to define the scope of their own commitments. The effect is less a cordon sanitaire around dangerous applications than a regulated theatre — reassuring to publics unequipped to evaluate the technical specifics, and convenient to actors who understand precisely what the frameworks do and do not require them to forgo.

Whether this represents a necessary first step toward genuine constraint, or merely the institutionalisation of the status quo under a more palatable name, is a question the field's architects have conspicuously declined to answer.

**In characterising current AI governance as a "regulated theatre," the author primarily implies that these frameworks**

**None**

options.label: A
